notes:
SCOPE: how privacy policy spread around the world outside the EU/US core. Contents: (1) "laws" — one record per country/territory for its first comprehensive (general, cross-sector or at least general public-sector) data-protection law: 93 jurisdictions across all eight regions; (2) 28 events (regional frameworks and turning points: Tokyo 1964, Bonn 1979, Israel 1981, Brazil 1988 and Argentina 1994 habeas data, Hong Kong 1995, Chile 1999, Cabo Verde 2001, Argentina adequacy 2003, APEC 2004/2011, Madrid 2009, ECOWAS 2010, Jerusalem PbD 2010, Uruguay/Convention 108 2013, UNGA 68/167 2013, Malabo 2014, Russia localisation 2014, HRC Special Rapporteur 2015, China CSL 2016 and PIPL 2021, Puttaswamy 2017, Convention 108+ 2018, Global CBPR 2022, Sri Lanka 2022, India DPDP 2023, Vietnam 2025, Greenleaf 172-country census 2025); (3) 15 frameworks side by side; (4) 6 policy models; (5) 7 myths; 11 quantities; 2 series (Greenleaf census by edition; new countries per decade).

DEFINITIONS: "first comprehensive law" = the first general statute on personal data (not a constitutional clause, not a sectoral law such as credit-reporting). Where the first general law covered only the public sector (Canada 1982/83, US 1974, Australia 1988 originally) or the private sector only (Japan 2003, Malaysia 2010, Singapore 2012, Mexico 2010), the note says so. Hesse (1970) is sub-national and appears in the Germany note; Sweden (1973) is the first national law. United States: record us-1974 is the Privacy Act (federal agencies only); the note explains there is no comprehensive federal law and that California's CCPA (2018) was the first comprehensive state law. Canada: record ca-1983 (Privacy Act, passed 1982, in force 1 July 1983) with PIPEDA (assented 13 April 2000) in the note; Canada's 1977 Human Rights Act Part IV privacy provisions are mentioned. Pakistan: no comprehensive law (DLA Piper: only PECA 2016 and a draft Personal Data Protection Bill) — no record, noted here. Coordinates for laws are the legislature (or the capital city), 4 decimals.

METHOD: every CONFIRMED quote was captured with tools/fetch-text.py and re-checked with --check (FOUND). Primary texts were used wherever a script could read them: legislation.gov.uk, laws-lois.justice.gc.ca, legislation.gov.au, irishstatutebook.ie, boe.es, finlex, zakonyprolidi.cz, bj.admin.ch, garanteprivacy.it, kremlin.ru, kvkk.gov.tr, argentina.gob.ar/infoleg, impo.com.uy, camara.leg.br, planalto.gov.br, secretariasenado.gov.co, diputados.gob.mx, joradp.dz, pdp.gov.bh, u.ae, gov.za, risa.gov.rw, dpa.gov.lk, meity.gov.in (gazette copy), law.moj.gov.tw, lawphil.net, mdes.go.th, npc.gov.cn, cac.gov.cn, pcpd.org.hk, documents.un.org, globalprivacyassembly.com, apec.org, asean.org, ITU (SADC), statewatch copy of the ECOWAS Act, redipd.org. Where official portals block scripts (Cloudflare 403 on coe.int, oecd.org, unctad.org, eur-lex; JS walls on many gazettes), DLA Piper's "Data Protection Laws of the World" country pages were used and marked CONFIRMED only where the page states the law and year; each DLA source carries a note flagging it as a secondary law-firm guide. About 45 of the 93 law records rest on DLA Piper alone. Several source records are reused verbatim from research/dataprotection.json and research/internet.json (Sweden, Germany/Hesse, Austria, Norway, Luxembourg, UK/ICO, New Zealand, US Privacy Act, OECD, Convention 108, EU Directive) so that slices agree.

NOT VERIFIED / KNOWN GAPS: (a) Council of Europe treaty office (coe.int, rm.coe.int) blocks scripts and the Internet Archive was intermittently unreachable, so current party counts for Convention 108 and 108+ are not verified at the primary (the Moldova "34th ratification" item is PENDING; 108+ entry-into-force threshold unverified). (b) UNCTAD's Global Cyberlaw Tracker (137/194 countries) could not be read (403); Greenleaf's PL&B census is used instead. (c) Greenleaf's SSRN papers and Global Tables are blocked (403); only free PL&B abstract pages were read, so series values come from those abstracts. (d) OHCHR blocks scripts: the name of the first Special Rapporteur (Joseph Cannataci) and HRC 28/16's adoption date (26 March 2015) are not quoted from a primary. (e) Zimbabwe's 2021 Act year is PENDING. (f) Denmark 1978 rests on a Luxembourg magazine (paperjam.lu) list of pioneers; Iceland (1981), Netherlands (1988), Portugal (1991), Belgium (1992), Hungary (1992), Greece (1997), Poland (1997), Slovenia, Estonia, Lithuania, Serbia, Albania, Moldova (2007), Oman (2022), Kuwait, Jamaica (2020), Bahamas (2003), Lesotho, Botswana (2018), Niger (2017), Togo, Mali and Pakistan are NOT in the laws table because no readable primary or dated secondary source was found in this pass. (g) Regulator names in the laws table are given for orientation and were not all verified against a quoted source. (h) Bangladesh's 2025 ordinance and Paraguay's 2025 law rest on press reports; the gazettes were not read. (i) The AU Malabo status list PDF's table columns are scrambled in the extracted text, so post-2023 ratification counts are not given. (j) The APEC 2004 release body (dateline Santiago, 20 November 2004) was read in raw HTML; only its headline is checked verbatim by the tool.

CORRECTIONS FOUND: the SADC Model Law on Data Protection is often dated 2010 but ITU's text records adoption by SADC ministers in November 2012 (myth sadc-model-law-2010). Hong Kong's PDPO is described by its regulator as "one of Asia's longest standing" comprehensive laws — the popular "Asia's first" claim was not asserted. Mexico's 2010 private-sector law was abrogated on 20 March 2025 and the INAI dissolved.

COORDINATION: Puttaswamy (2017), Convention 108 (1981), OECD (1980), the EU Directive and GDPR may also appear in other slices; ids here are distinct (india-supreme-court-puttaswamy-privacy-fundamental-right-2017, frameworks coe-convention-108-1981, oecd-privacy-guidelines-1980, eu-data-protection-directive-1995, eu-general-data-protection-regulation-2016) and the editorial layer should de-duplicate.

events.title: A Tokyo court recognises a right to privacy in the "After the Banquet" case
events.place: Tokyo District Court, Kasumigaseki, Tokyo, Japan
events.summary: Ruling on a suit over Yukio Mishima's novel Utage no Ato (After the Banquet), which was modelled on the lives of real people, the Tokyo District Court defined privacy as the right not to have one's private life publicised without authorisation. The judgment (15-9 Kaminshu 2317) came shortly after Japanese scholars had introduced the American 'right to be let alone' theory in the early 1960s.
events.significance: Shows a court outside Europe and the United States taking up the American idea of privacy and making it an enforceable right in 1964, six years before the first data-protection statute (Hesse, 1970) and nearly four decades before Japan's general Act on the Protection of Personal Information (2003).

sources.institution: Japan Institute for Labour Policy and Training (JILPT) — Ryoko Sakuraba, Kobe University
sources.title: Protection of Personal Information and Privacy in the Japanese Workplace (JILPT Report No. 14)
sources.quote: the Tokyo District Court defined privacy as the right [of the individuals concerned] not to have their private lives publicized in an unauthorized way … Tokyo District Court (28 September 1964), 15-9 Kaminshu 2317.
sources.note: The PDF text layer drops apostrophes. The plaintiff, former foreign minister Hachiro Arita, is named in secondary accounts but not in this source; not asserted here.

events.locationNote: Tokyo District Court building, Kasumigaseki (current courthouse site).

issues: Significance claimed the ruling came 'decades before the first data-protection statutes'. The first data-protection statute (Hesse) dates from 1970, only six years later. 'Decades' holds only for Japan's own general law, the Act on the Protection of Personal Information of 2003, which the same JILPT paper cites.

Significance also said the ruling undercut 'the idea that privacy law is a purely Western export', but the record's own summary and source say Japan adopted the American 'right to be let alone' after scholars imported it (the paper cites Masami Ito, 1963). The ruling shows a US idea adopted and made enforceable in Japan, not a home-grown alternative. Reworded.

All other claims check out. The date 28 September 1964 and the citation 15-9 Kaminshu 2317 are in the source. Japanese case-law summaries independently give 東京地判昭和39年9月28日 and name the plaintiff as 有田八郎 (Hachiro Arita), and they describe the right protected as 私生活をみだりに公開されない権利 ('the right not to have one's private life disclosed without good reason'). 'Early 1960s' fits the Ito (1963) footnote. The coordinates match the Tokyo District Court at Kasumigaseki 1-1-4.

events.title: Data-protection commissioners hold their first international conference in Bonn
events.place: Bonn, Federal Republic of Germany (host: Federal Commissioner for Data Protection)
events.summary: The first international conference of data-protection and privacy commissioners met in Bonn in 1979 at the invitation of West Germany's Federal Commissioner for Data Protection; the second met in Ottawa. For its first 20 years the conference met mostly in Europe: the Assembly's own list shows only four of the 20 meetings before 1999 held elsewhere (Ottawa 1980, Quebec 1987, Sydney 1992 and Ottawa 1996), although its history page puts the figure at five. At its 2019 conference in Tirana it adopted the name Global Privacy Assembly.
events.significance: Created the regulators' own global forum, the body that later wrote international privacy standards (Madrid 2009) and endorsed Privacy by Design (Jerusalem 2010).

sources.title: History of the Assembly
sources.quote: The Assembly first met in Bonn, Germany, in 1979 and then crossed the Atlantic for its second meeting in Ottawa, Canada.

sources.institution: Federal Commissioner for Data Protection and Freedom of Information (BfDI), Germany
sources.title: Global Privacy Assembly
sources.quote: The first international conference was held in Bonn in 1979 at the invitation of the then Federal Commissioner for Data Protection.

sources.title: History of the Assembly
sources.quote: The Assembly met for the first 20 years primarily in European locations with an occasional foray to Canada and one trip down-under to Sydney, Australia, in 1992.

sources.title: History of the Assembly — list of all previous Conferences
sources.quote: 20 th International Conference – Santiago de Compostella, Spain, 1998 19 th International Conference – Brussels, Belgium, 1997 18 th International Conference – Ottawa, Canada, 1996 17 th International Conference – Copenhagen, Denmark, 1995 16 th International Conference – The Hague, Netherlands, 1994 15 th International Conference – Manchester, United Kingdom, 1993 14 th International Conference – Sydney, Australia, 1992 13 th International Conference – Strasbourg, France, 1991 12 th International Conference – Paris, France, 1990 11 th International Conference – Berlin, F.R.Germany, 1989 10 th International Conference – Oslo, Norway, 1988 9 th International Conference – Quebec, Canada, 1987 8 th International Conference – Lisbon, Portugal, 1986 7 th International Conference – Luxembourg, 1985 6 th International Conference – Vienna, Austria, 1984 5 th International Conference – Stockholm, Sweden, 1983 4 th International Conference – London, United Kingdom, 1982 3 rd International Conference – Paris, France, 1981 2 nd International Conference – Ottawa, Canada, 1980 1 st International Conference – Bonn, F.R.Germany, 1979
sources.note: --check FOUND. This is the page's full list of conferences 1 to 20 (1979 to 1998). Four were held outside Europe: 2nd Ottawa 1980, 9th Quebec 1987, 14th Sydney 1992 and 18th Ottawa 1996. The 21st, in Hong Kong in 1999, falls outside the 'before 1999' window.

sources.institution: Federal Commissioner for Data Protection and Freedom of Information (BfDI), Germany
sources.title: Global Privacy Assembly
sources.quote: At the conference 2019 in Tirana, Albania, it adopted the new name of "Global Privacy Assembly ( GPA )".
sources.note: --check FOUND. Supports the 2019 Tirana renaming.

events.locationNote: Bonn, then West Germany's seat of government and home of the Federal Commissioner; exact venue not stated in sources.

issues: Number is contradicted by the source's own data. The summary says 'only five of the 20 meetings before 1999 were held elsewhere' than Europe, copying the GPA history page's prose ('Of the 20 conferences before 1999, only five were held outside Europe'). The same page lists all 20 conferences from 1979 to 1998, and only four were outside Europe: Ottawa 1980, Quebec 1987, Sydney 1992 and Ottawa 1996. The page's own prose agrees with four: 'an occasional foray to Canada and one trip down-under to Sydney'. The figure of five appears only if the 21st conference (Hong Kong, 1999) is counted.
The Tirana 2019 renaming had no source. Added the BfDI page, which states it.

Everything else checks out. Bonn 1979 was the first meeting and Ottawa the second, and the BfDI invited it. Madrid 2009 (international standards) and Jerusalem 2010 (Privacy by Design resolution) are accurate, and the GPA page confirms the Madrid resolution and that the Executive Committee was set up in Jerusalem in 2010. The Bonn coordinates are fine given the stated venue uncertainty.

events.title: Brazil's new constitution creates habeas data
events.place: Congresso Nacional, Brasília, Brazil
events.summary: Brazil's 1988 Constitution, published in the Diário Oficial on 5 October 1988, created a remedy called habeas data (Art. 5, LXXII): a person may go to court to learn what information about them is held in records or data banks of government agencies or entities of a public character, and to have it corrected. It was written as the country emerged from two decades of military rule.
events.significance: Established a Latin American model in which the individual's right to see and correct data held about them is a constitutional writ rather than a regulator's rulebook.

sources.institution: Câmara dos Deputados (Chamber of Deputies), Brazil
sources.title: Constituição de 1988 — Publicação Original
sources.quote: para assegurar o conhecimento de informações relativas à pessoa do impetrante, constantes de registros ou bancos de dados de entidades governamentais ou de caráter público;
sources.note: Art. 5, LXXII(a). Translation: 'to ensure knowledge of information relating to the person of the petitioner, contained in records or data banks of government entities or entities of a public character'. The page also records publication in the Diário Oficial da União, Seção 1, 5/10/1988.

sources.institution: Constitute Project (translation by Keith S. Rosenn)
sources.title: Brazil's Constitution of 1988 with Amendments through 2017
sources.quote: habeas data shall be granted: to assure knowledge of personal information about the petitioner contained in records or data banks of government agencies or entities of a public character

events.locationNote: Seat of the National Constituent Assembly (National Congress, Brasília).

issues: No errors found. Art. 5, LXXII was confirmed in the raw HTML of the Câmara page: 'LXXII - conceder-se-á habeas data: a) para assegurar o conhecimento de informações relativas à pessoa do impetrante ... b) para a retificação de dados ...'. The page records 'Diário Oficial da União - Seção 1 - 5/10/1988, Página 1 (Publicação Original)'. The Constitute Project (Rosenn) translation is verbatim. 'Two decades of military rule' (1964 to 1985) is accurate general history; no source in the record states it. The coordinates match the Congresso Nacional in Brasília.

events.title: Argentina writes habeas data into its reformed constitution
events.place: Convención Nacional Constituyente, Santa Fe, Argentina
events.summary: The 1994 reform of Argentina's constitution, sanctioned by the Constituent Convention in the city of Santa Fe on 22 August 1994, added a new Article 43 whose third paragraph gives every person a habeas data action: the right to learn what data about them is held in public registers or in private databanks that supply reports, and to demand its deletion, correction, confidentiality or updating where it is false or discriminatory. The European Commission later described this habeas data remedy as making data protection a fundamental right in Argentina.
events.significance: Joined the wave of new Latin American constitutions that took up Brazil's habeas data (Colombia 1991, Paraguay 1992, Peru 1993). Like Colombia's and Paraguay's, it reached private databanks, and it became the foundation on which Argentina built its 2000 data-protection law.

sources.institution: Government of Argentina — Información Legislativa (Ley 24.430, texto ordenado de la Constitución Nacional)
sources.title: Constitución de la Nación Argentina
sources.quote: Toda persona podrá interponer esta acción para tomar conocimiento de los datos a ella referidos y de su finalidad, que consten en registros o bancos de datos públicos, o los privados destinados a proveer informes
sources.note: Art. 43, third paragraph. Translation: 'Any person may bring this action to learn of the data referring to them and its purpose, held in public registers or databanks, or private ones intended to supply reports'. The same page closes: 'DADA EN LA SALA DE SESIONES DE LA CONVENCIÓN NACIONAL CONSTITUYENTE, EN LA CIUDAD DE SANTA FE, A LOS VEINTIDÓS DÍAS DEL MES DE AGOSTO DEL AÑO MIL NOVECIENTOS NOVENTA Y CUATRO.'

sources.institution: European Commission (Official Journal L 168, 5 July 2003), read via Internet Archive copy of EUR-Lex
sources.title: Commission Decision 2003/490/EC of 30 June 2003 on the adequate protection of personal data in Argentina
sources.quote: This is a subcategory of the procedure enshrined in the Constitution for the protection of constitutional rights and therefore makes the protection of personal data a fundamental right.
sources.note: EUR-Lex itself returns a bot challenge to scripts; canonical URL https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32003D0490

sources.institution: Constitute Project (translation by Max Planck Institute, with updates by the Comparative Constitutions Project)
sources.title: Colombia's Constitution of 1991 with Amendments through 2015
sources.quote: individuals have the right to know, update, and rectify information collected about them in data banks and in the records of public and private entities.
sources.note: --check FOUND. Art. 15, first paragraph (1991 text). Shows that data-access and correction rights reaching private entities predate Argentina's 1994 reform.

sources.institution: Constitute Project (translation by Maria del Carmen Gress, © William S. Hein & Co.)
sources.title: Paraguay's Constitution of 1992 with Amendments through 2011
sources.quote: All persons may access the information and the data that about themselves, or about their assets, [that] is [obren] in official or private registries of a public character
sources.note: --check FOUND. Art. 135 'Of Habeas Data' (1992).

sources.title: Peru's Constitution of 1993 with Amendments through 2021
sources.quote: The writ of habeas data, which operates in case of an act or omission by any authority, official, or person that violates or threatens the rights referred to in article 2, subparagraphs 5, and 6 of this Constitution.
sources.note: --check FOUND. Art. 200(3) (1993 constitution).

events.locationNote: The 1994 Constituent Convention sat in Santa Fe (with sessions also in Paraná); coordinates are Santa Fe city.

issues: The summary says the reform 'added to Article 43' a right, which implies Article 43 already existed. In fact Article 43 as a whole (amparo, with habeas data in its third paragraph) was new in 1994. It sits in the chapter 'Nuevos derechos y garantías' (arts. 36 to 43) that the reform created.

Significance overstated Argentina's role. The habeas data model had already spread from Brazil to Colombia (1991 Constitution, Art. 15, which covers 'public and private entities'), Paraguay (1992, Art. 135 'Del habeas data', which covers 'official or private registries of a public character') and Peru (1993, Art. 200(3)). So Argentina neither 'carried the habeas data model ... across Latin America' nor was first to extend it to private databanks.

Source 0 date: the cited page is the Ley 24.430 official-text publication (Boletín Oficial 10-01-1995), not a 22 August 1994 document. The constitutional text it reproduces is dated 22 August 1994 in Santa Fe.

Confirmed: the text of the third paragraph of Art. 43 (including 'supresión, rectificación, confidencialidad o actualización' in case of 'falsedad o discriminación'); 'DADA ... EN LA CIUDAD DE SANTA FE, A LOS VEINTIDÓS DÍAS DEL MES DE AGOSTO ... 1994'; the Convention sitting in Santa Fe and Paraná (Ley 24.430 art. 2); and recital 7 of Decision 2003/490/EC calling habeas data a fundamental right.

events.title: Argentina becomes the first Latin American country the EU deems 'adequate'
events.place: European Commission (Breydel building, while the Berlaymont was being renovated), Brussels, Belgium
events.summary: On 30 June 2003 the European Commission decided, under Article 25(6) of Directive 95/46/EC, that for the purposes of Article 25(2) Argentina provides an adequate level of protection for personal data transferred from the European Community. The decision rested on Argentina's constitutional habeas data remedy and its Personal Data Protection Act No 25.326 of 4 October 2000.
events.significance: One of the first demonstrations that a country outside Europe could secure the free flow of European data by adopting a European-style omnibus law, a lever that spread the EU model worldwide.

sources.institution: European Commission (Official Journal L 168, 5 July 2003), read via Internet Archive copy of EUR-Lex
sources.title: Commission Decision 2003/490/EC of 30 June 2003 on the adequate protection of personal data in Argentina
sources.quote: For the purposes of Article 25(2) of Directive 95/46/EC, Argentina is regarded as providing an adequate level of protection for personal data transferred from the Community.
sources.note: Canonical URL https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32003D0490 (bot-walled to scripts).

sources.institution: European Commission (Official Journal L 168, 5 July 2003), read via Internet Archive copy of EUR-Lex
sources.title: Commission Decision 2003/490/EC — recital 8
sources.quote: The Personal Data Protection Act No 25.326 of 4 October 2000 (hereinafter "the Act") develops and widens the Constitutional provisions.

sources.title: Adequacy decisions
sources.quote: The European Commission has so far recognised: Andorra , Argentina , Brazil , Canada (commercial organisations), Faroe Islands , Guernsey , Israel , Isle of Man , Japan , Jersey , New Zealand , Republic of Korea , Switzerland ,
sources.note: --check FOUND. The full list continues with the UK, the US (DPF), Uruguay and the European Patent Organisation. The only Latin American countries are Argentina (2003/490/EC), Uruguay (2012) and Brazil (2026), which supports 'first Latin American'.

events.locationNote: The Commission's temporary headquarters from 1991 to 2004 was the Breydel building, Avenue d'Auderghem; the decision itself is 'Done at Brussels'.

issues: Legal basis misstated. The summary says the Commission 'decided under Article 25(2)'. The decision was adopted under Article 25(6) of Directive 95/46/EC ('in particular Article 25(6) thereof'). Article 1 finds Argentina adequate 'for the purposes of Article 25(2)', which is the provision listing the factors for assessing adequacy.

Place is anachronistic. The Commission was out of the Berlaymont from 1991 to 2004 for asbestos removal and renovation, and was based in the Breydel building (Wikipedia: 'temporary headquarters for the European Commission between 1991 and 2004'). The decision says only 'Done at Brussels'. Place and coordinates changed to the Breydel building (50.8400, 4.3850).

Significance overclaims. Argentina did not first 'show' that a non-European country could gain access to European data flows: Canada's adequacy decision (2002/2/EC, 20 December 2001) came earlier. 'Buy access' is loaded wording. Reworded.

Title 'first Latin American country' confirmed. The Commission's current adequacy list names only three Latin American countries: Argentina (2003), Uruguay (2012) and Brazil (2026). Confirmed: 30 June 2003; OJ L 168, 5.7.2003, p. 19–22; Act 25.326 of 4 October 2000; the habeas data basis (recital 7).

events.title: UN General Assembly: privacy rights apply online too
events.place: Temporary General Assembly Hall, North Lawn Building, United Nations Headquarters, New York, United States
events.summary: Six months after the Snowden disclosures, the UN General Assembly adopted resolution 68/167, 'The right to privacy in the digital age', on 18 December 2013. It affirmed that the rights people have offline must also be protected online, including the right to privacy, and called on all states to respect and protect privacy in digital communication.
events.significance: The General Assembly's first resolution on the right to privacy in the digital age, a response to revelations of mass surveillance; it asked the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights for a report on surveillance, interception and data collection, including on a mass scale.

sources.title: A/RES/68/167 — The right to privacy in the digital age
sources.quote: Affirms that the same rights that people have offline must also be protected online, including the right to privacy
sources.note: Document header: 'Resolution adopted by the General Assembly on 18 December 2013'; distributed 21 January 2014.

sources.title: A/RES/68/167 — The right to privacy in the digital age
sources.quote: Resolution adopted by the General Assembly on 18 December 2013

sources.title: A/RES/68/167 — The right to privacy in the digital age
sources.quote: Requests the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights to submit a report on the protection and promotion of the right to privacy in the context of domestic and extraterritorial surveillance and/or the interception of digital communications and the collection of personal data, including on a mass scale
sources.note: Operative paragraph 5; supports the revised significance.

sources.title: United Nations General Assembly Building
sources.quote: During the project, the General Assembly met at a temporary building on the UN headquarters' North Lawn.
sources.note: The preceding sentence gives the closure date, 'The General Assembly Building was closed for renovations on May 31, 2013.', and a later one says 'When the building reopened in September 2014'. Both FOUND. Supports the venue correction.

events.locationNote: UN Headquarters, New York. The General Assembly Building was closed for renovation from May 2013 to September 2014, so the Assembly met in the temporary North Lawn Building.

issues: Wrong venue. The General Assembly Building closed for renovation on 31 May 2013 and reopened in September 2014; in between, the General Assembly met in a temporary building on the UN headquarters' North Lawn. The 70th plenary meeting of 18 December 2013 cannot have sat in the 'United Nations General Assembly Hall'. Coordinates (UN HQ campus) are close enough.

Significance overstates. Digital and data privacy were already on the UN human-rights agenda: Human Rights Committee General Comment 16 (1988) and the General Assembly's 1990 Guidelines for the Regulation of Computerized Personal Data Files. There was also no African regional treaty yet in December 2013; the Malabo Convention came in June 2014. What is new in 68/167 is that it is the Assembly's first resolution on privacy in the digital age, responding to mass surveillance, and that it commissioned a report from the High Commissioner.

Checked and correct: adopted 18 December 2013 (70th plenary meeting); document distributed 21 January 2014; 'Affirms that the same rights that people have offline must also be protected online, including the right to privacy'; paragraph 4(a) 'To respect and protect the right to privacy, including in the context of digital communication'. All quotes FOUND.

events.title: The UN creates a Special Rapporteur on the right to privacy
events.place: Human Rights Council, Palais des Nations, Geneva, Switzerland
events.summary: The UN Human Rights Council's resolution 28/16, 'The right to privacy in the digital age', adopted without a vote on 26 March 2015, decided to appoint for three years a special rapporteur on the right to privacy, tasked among other things with gathering information on international and national frameworks and practices. It was the first UN mandate dedicated to privacy. The first mandate-holder, Joseph Cannataci of Malta, was selected in July 2015, and his mandate began on 1 August 2015.
events.significance: Gave privacy a standing independent monitor inside the UN human-rights system, reporting on surveillance and data practices worldwide.

sources.title: A/HRC/RES/28/16 — The right to privacy in the digital age
sources.quote: Decides to appoint, for a period of three years, a special rapporteur on the right to privacy
sources.note: Distributed 1 April 2015. The final page records adoption at the Council's '56th meeting 26 March 2015 [Adopted without a vote.]'. The first mandate-holder, Joseph Cannataci of Malta, is named in the EPIC and EFF sources added to this record.

sources.title: A/HRC/31/64 — Report of the Special Rapporteur on the right to privacy
sources.quote: since it was prepared scarcely six months after the appointment of the Special Rapporteur on 1 August 2015

sources.title: A/HRC/RES/28/16 — The right to privacy in the digital age
sources.quote: 56th meeting 26 March 2015 [Adopted without a vote.]
sources.note: Adoption line at the end of the resolution (page 4). --check FOUND.

sources.title: A/HRC/31/64 — Report of the Special Rapporteur on the right to privacy
sources.quote: since the mandate commenced on 1 August 2015
sources.note: Para 42. --check FOUND.

sources.title: EFF Welcomes The United Nations' New Privacy Watchdog
sources.quote: The Electronic Frontier Foundation welcomes the appointment of Mr. Joseph Cannataci as the first-ever UN Special Rapporteur on the Right to Privacy.
sources.note: The next sentence, also FOUND, reads: 'The President of the UN Human Rights Council (HRC) appointed Mr. Cannataci last week following the March 2015 HRC resolution'. The page is dated July 8, 2015.

sources.title: UN Appoints Special Rapporteur on Right to Privacy
sources.quote: The President of the UN Human Rights Council has selected Mr. Joseph Cannataci to serve as the first UN Special Rapporteur on the Right to Privacy.
sources.note: The page is dated 'July 3, 2015' (FOUND). EPIC's president Marc Rotenberg was one of the candidates for the post.

events.locationNote: Palais des Nations, Geneva.

issues: Source 0's note wrongly says the adoption date is not in the resolution and marks it '(PENDING)'. The last page of A/HRC/RES/28/16 reads '56th meeting 26 March 2015 [Adopted without a vote.]' (FOUND), so 26 March 2015 is confirmed by the primary source. The note is corrected and a source for the adoption line is added.

The summary says the first mandate-holder 'was appointed on 1 August 2015'. That is imprecise. The HRC President selected Joseph Cannataci on 3 July 2015 (EPIC, dated July 3, 2015; EFF, 8 July 2015: 'appointed Mr. Cannataci last week'). 1 August 2015 is the date the mandate began: A/HRC/31/64 para 42 says 'the mandate commenced on 1 August 2015'. Para 3 of the same report loosely calls it 'the appointment ... on 1 August 2015'. The sentence is reworded.

'It was the first UN mandate dedicated to privacy' had no source. EFF ('the first-ever UN Special Rapporteur on the Right to Privacy') and EPIC ('the first UN Special Rapporteur on the Right to Privacy') support it, so both are added.

Checked and correct: resolution number and title, the three-year term (verbatim), the task of gathering information 'including on international and national frameworks, national practices and experience' (verbatim), the Distr. date of 1 April 2015, the A/HRC/31/64 Distr. date of 24 November 2016, and the Palais des Nations coordinates. Both existing quotes were re-fetched with a cleared cache and FOUND.

events.title: African Union adopts the Malabo Convention on cyber security and personal data
events.place: 23rd AU Assembly, Malabo, Equatorial Guinea
events.summary: The African Union Convention on Cyber Security and Personal Data Protection was adopted on 27 June 2014 at the 23rd AU Assembly of Heads of State and Government in Malabo. It covers personal-data protection, electronic commerce and cyber security, and entered into force on 8 June 2023 after the required fifteenth ratification, deposited by Mauritania.
events.significance: Africa's continental treaty on personal data, following ECOWAS's regional act of 2010; it made harmonised national laws a continental goal, though it took nine years to gather the fifteen ratifications needed to enter into force.

events.title: Hong Kong enacts one of Asia's earliest comprehensive privacy laws
events.place: Legislative Council Building (now the Court of Final Appeal), Central, Hong Kong
events.summary: Hong Kong's Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance was enacted on 3 August 1995 and came into force on 20 December 1996, shortly before the handover to China; an independent regulator, the Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data, was set up on 1 August 1996. It grew from a 1994 Law Reform Commission report that recommended a law based on the OECD's 1980 Privacy Guidelines, partly so that Hong Kong would keep an 'adequate' level of protection as a trading centre.
events.significance: An early Asian omnibus law covering both government and business, adopted partly to secure an 'adequate' level of data protection so that Hong Kong could keep its standing as an international trading centre.

Confirmed: enacted 3 August 1995; in force 20 December 1996 (Wikisource commencement notes show that Part II and s.71 started on 1 August 1996, ss.30 and 33 were excepted, and s.33 later took effect on 1 August 1997); and PCPD's own wording 'one of Asia’s longest standing comprehensive data protection laws'.

events.title: APEC ministers endorse the APEC Privacy Framework
events.place: APEC Ministerial Meeting, Santiago, Chile
events.summary: Meeting in Santiago on 17–18 November 2004, APEC ministers endorsed a Privacy Framework submitted by the chair of the forum's Electronic Commerce Steering Group; it was published in 2005. Consistent with the OECD's 1980 guidelines, it promoted privacy protection that avoided 'unnecessary barriers to information flows', and it was voluntary: member economies could give effect to it through legislation, administrative measures or industry self-regulation.
events.significance: Set up the Asia-Pacific's trade-first, accountability-based alternative to the EU's rights-based model.

Both the AMM agenda paper 2004/AMM/014rev1 and the 2004 AMM statement page (dated 17 November; ministers 'gathered in Santiago, Chile, on 17-18 November 2004') say so. 20 November 2004 is only the dateline of the APEC news release that reported the endorsement afterwards, and the Leaders' meeting ran 20–21 November.
'Drafted by the forum's Electronic Commerce Steering Group' is not stated in either cited source. The AMM paper does state 'Submitted by: ECSG Chair', which supports it, so that source is added.

Consistent with the OECD 1980 Guidelines. Implementation is flexible and can be legislative, administrative or industry self-regulatory. Both existing quotes re-fetched and FOUND. Santiago coordinates are correct.

events.title: APEC leaders endorse the Cross-Border Privacy Rules system
events.place: APEC Leaders' Meeting, Honolulu, Hawaii, United States
events.summary: On 13 November 2011 in Honolulu, President Obama and representatives of the other APEC economies endorsed the Cross-Border Privacy Rules (CBPR), a voluntary but enforceable code of conduct under which companies are certified by third parties, with privacy authorities acting as backstop enforcers. On 25 July 2012 the United States became the system's first formal participant and the FTC its first enforcement authority.
events.significance: Turned APEC's principles into a certification market: the company, vetted by an accountability agent, writes and is held to its own privacy rules.

issues: No factual errors. Both FTC releases re-fetched; both quotes FOUND. The 2011 release confirms review and certification by third parties and privacy authorities as 'backstop enforcers'. The 2012 release confirms 'a voluntary but enforceable code of conduct' and approval on July 25. The Honolulu Leaders' Declaration independently commits to 'Implement the APEC Cross Border Privacy Rules System'; it was read in the apec.org raw HTML, but its body is not extractable by the verbatim tool.

events.title: Seven economies take the CBPR system global
events.place: US Department of Commerce, Washington, DC, United States
events.summary: On 21 April 2022 Canada, Japan, the Republic of Korea, the Philippines, Singapore, Chinese Taipei and the United States, seven of the nine economies then participating in APEC's CBPR system, declared the establishment of a Global CBPR Forum. Its aim is an international certification system based on the APEC CBPR and Privacy Recognition for Processors systems, open beyond APEC. The other two CBPR economies, Australia and Mexico, did not sign the April declaration, but the Forum now counts all nine as its founders.
events.significance: Positioned company certification, not individual rights or person-set terms, as the rival global model for data transfers to the EU's adequacy system.

events.title: World privacy regulators welcome the 'Madrid Resolution' on international standards
events.place: 31st International Conference of Data Protection and Privacy Commissioners, Madrid, Spain
events.summary: On 5 November 2009 the International Conference of Data Protection and Privacy Commissioners, meeting in Madrid, welcomed a Joint Proposal for a Draft of International Standards on the Protection of Privacy with regard to the processing of Personal Data. Coordinated by the Spanish Data Protection Agency, it was drafted through the joint efforts of privacy authorities from fifty countries and sought to integrate legislation from five continents into one set of principles and rights.
events.significance: The first attempt by the world's regulators to write a single global rulebook, a step toward a common vocabulary that machine-readable terms could later reference.

events.title: The world's privacy regulators adopt Privacy by Design
events.place: 32nd International Conference of Data Protection and Privacy Commissioners, Jerusalem
events.summary: The 32nd International Conference of Data Protection and Privacy Commissioners, meeting in Jerusalem on 27–29 October 2010, resolved to recognise Privacy by Design as an essential component of fundamental privacy protection. Its seven foundational principles include 'Privacy as the Default' and 'Respect for User Privacy', and the resolution accepted that regulation and policy alone were not sufficient to safeguard privacy.
events.significance: Moved regulators from rules on paper toward privacy engineered into systems, the lineage in which person-side, machine-readable terms sit.

events.title: China adopts its Cybersecurity Law
events.place: Standing Committee of the National People's Congress, Great Hall of the People, Beijing, China
events.summary: The Standing Committee of China's National People's Congress adopted the Cybersecurity Law on 7 November 2016, and it took effect on 1 June 2017. The law firm DLA Piper describes it as the first national-level law to address both cybersecurity and data-privacy protection. Its Article 37 required operators of critical information infrastructure to store within China the personal information and important data they collect and generate in their operations there, and to pass a security assessment before any necessary transfer abroad.
events.significance: Established a template in which personal-data rules are bound up with state security and data sovereignty.

The law text continues on pages 2 and 3 of the same CAC article (c_1119867116_2.htm and c_1119867116_3.htm), where Articles 37 and 79 are quoted in the sources added to this record.

issues: The DLA Piper quote was truncated mid-word ('data privacy prot'). The page carries the full sentence, and the quote is replaced with it (FOUND).

Source 0's note says the CAC page shows only the first part of the law, so the Article 37 localisation duty was 'summarised from the DLA Piper overview'. In fact the CAC article continues on c_1119867116_2.htm and _3.htm. Article 37 (page 2) and Article 79 on the effective date (page 3) were both read there verbatim and are added as primary sources.

The summary understated Article 37. It covers 'personal information and important data' that critical-information-infrastructure operators collect and generate in their operations inside China, and it requires a security assessment before any necessary transfer abroad. The summary is refined.

'The first national-level law addressing both cyber security and the protection of personal information' is DLA Piper's characterisation. An earlier national-level instrument on personal electronic information existed (the NPC Standing Committee's 2012 Decision on Strengthening Network Information Protection, a decision rather than a law). The claim is now attributed rather than stated as bare fact.

events.title: China adopts the Personal Information Protection Law (PIPL)
events.place: Standing Committee of the National People's Congress, Great Hall of the People, Beijing, China
events.summary: China's Personal Information Protection Law was adopted by the NPC Standing Committee on 20 August 2021 and took effect on 1 November 2021. It gives individuals rights to access, copy, correct and erase their data, and Article 40 requires critical-infrastructure operators and large processors to store personal information collected in China domestically, with security assessments for exports.
events.significance: Gave the world's largest online population GDPR-like individual rights inside a state-security framework, showing that 'omnibus law' does not mean one political model.

events.title: India's Supreme Court declares privacy a fundamental right
events.place: Supreme Court of India, Tilak Marg, New Delhi, India
events.summary: In Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd) v. Union of India, decided on 24 August 2017, a nine-judge bench held that the right to privacy is protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and the freedoms of Part III of the Constitution. The reference arose from a constitutional challenge to Aadhaar, the national biometric identity database; the court noted that the government had set up a committee under Justice B.N. Srikrishna to review data-protection norms.
events.significance: Made privacy a constitutional right for 1.3 billion people and set India on the road to its Digital Personal Data Protection Act of 2023.

Quote 1 is para 185 of Chandrachud J's plurality opinion. Quote 2 does open Bobde J's separate opinion ('S. A. BOBDE, J. The Origin of the Reference 1. ...'), so the attribution is correct.

events.title: Russia orders citizens' personal data stored on Russian soil
events.place: Moscow Kremlin (signing), Moscow, Russia
events.summary: Federal Law No. 242-FZ of 21 July 2014 amended Russia's personal-data law to require operators collecting personal data, including over the internet, to record, systematise, accumulate, store, update and retrieve the personal data of Russian citizens using databases located in the Russian Federation, subject to a few exceptions. After an amendment brought the date forward by a year, it took effect on 1 September 2015.
events.significance: The emblematic data-localisation law: privacy law used as an instrument of territorial sovereignty over data.

sources.note: Translation: 'the operator is obliged to ensure the recording, systematisation, accumulation, storage, clarification (updating, changing) and retrieval of personal data of citizens of the Russian Federation using databases located in the territory of the Russian Federation'.

sources.title: Федеральный закон от 21.07.2014 г. № 242-ФЗ — Статья 4
sources.quote: Настоящий Федеральный закон вступает в силу с 1 сентября 2015 года. (В редакции Федерального закона от 31.12.2014 № 526-ФЗ)
sources.note: Translation: 'This Federal Law enters into force on 1 September 2015 (as amended by Federal Law No. 526-FZ of 31.12.2014)'. The original text set 1 September 2016.

sources.title: Федеральный закон от 21.07.2014 г. № 242-ФЗ
sources.quote: Президент Российской Федерации В.Путин Москва, Кремль 21 июля 2014 года № 242-ФЗ
sources.note: Translation: 'President of the Russian Federation V. Putin, Moscow, Kremlin, 21 July 2014, No. 242-FZ'. Supports the date and the place of signing.

events.locationNote: Signed into law by the President in Moscow; coordinates are the Kremlin.

issues: Paraphrase too broad. The law lists specific operations: recording, systematisation, accumulation, storage, clarification (updating, changing) and retrieval ('запись, систематизацию, накопление, хранение, уточнение (обновление, изменение), извлечение'). It does not say 'process' in general; 'обработка' covers wider operations such as transfer, which the article does not localise. It also carves out exceptions (Art. 6(1) points 2, 3, 4, 8).

Checked and correct: signed 'Москва, Кремль 21 июля 2014 года № 242-ФЗ' (FOUND). Passed by the State Duma on 4 July 2014 and approved by the Federation Council on 9 July 2014. Article 4 as amended by 526-FZ of 31.12.2014 gives entry into force on 1 September 2015. The original 1 September 2016 date is confirmed by secondary sources (ZwillGen, Suffolk JHTL). Kremlin coordinates are correct. Both quotes re-fetched and FOUND.

events.title: Vietnam passes its first Personal Data Protection Law
events.place: National Assembly of Vietnam, Ba Dinh, Hanoi
events.summary: Vietnam's National Assembly passed Law No. 91/2025/QH15 on Personal Data Protection on 26 June 2025, raising the country's rules from a 2023 government decree to a statute; it took effect on 1 January 2026. It sets out rights for citizens to be informed, to consent, and to access, correct and request deletion of their data.
events.significance: One of the newest national laws, showing the omnibus model still spreading in the age of AI.

sources.institution: Báo Điện tử Chính phủ (Government of Vietnam e-newspaper)
sources.title: Luật Bảo vệ dữ liệu cá nhân chính thức có hiệu lực từ ngày mai (1/1/2026)
sources.quote: Được Quốc hội thông qua ngày 26/6/2025, Luật Bảo vệ dữ liệu cá nhân đã xác lập rõ các quyền dữ liệu cơ bản của công dân, bao gồm quyền được biết, quyền đồng ý, quyền truy cập, chỉnh sửa và yêu cầu xóa dữ liệu.
sources.note: Translation: 'Passed by the National Assembly on 26/6/2025, the Law on Personal Data Protection clearly establishes citizens' basic data rights, including the right to be informed, the right to consent, the right to access, correct and request deletion of data.' Headline: 'The Law on Personal Data Protection officially takes effect tomorrow (1/1/2026)'.

sources.title: Data Protection Laws of the World — Vietnam
sources.quote: On 26 June 2025, Law No. 91/2025/QH15 on Personal Data Protection (“PDPL”) was officially enacted by the National Assembly and took effect on 1 January 2026. This elevated the regulatory framework from decree-level provisions to statutory law.

sources.title: Data Protection Laws of the World — Vietnam
sources.quote: Decree 356 formally announced the replacement of the Decree No. 13/2023/ND-CP of the Government dated 17 April 2023 on Personal Data Protection
sources.note: Identifies the 2023 decree that the 2025 statute superseded. --check FOUND.

events.locationNote: National Assembly House, Hanoi.

issues: Both quotes re-fetched with a cleared cache and FOUND. Báo Điện tử Chính phủ article dated 2025-12-31 (datePublished 2025-12-31T15:58+07:00), matching the source date.

Checked and correct: Law No. 91/2025/QH15 passed 26 June 2025, in force 1 January 2026. The listed rights (informed, consent, access, correction, deletion) are verbatim in translation. 'Raising the country's rules from a 2023 government decree' is supported: DLA Piper names the replaced instrument as Decree No. 13/2023/ND-CP of 17 April 2023 (FOUND), and that source is added. The Hanoi coordinates are right.

events.title: Israel passes the Protection of Privacy Law
events.place: Knesset, Jerusalem
events.summary: Israel's Protection of Privacy Law, 5741-1981, made infringement of privacy both a civil wrong and, in its wilful forms, a criminal offence, and added rules for registering and running databases. Enacted soon after the OECD's 1980 Privacy Guidelines, it was one of the world's first attempts at a comprehensive statutory privacy framework. It was overhauled by Amendment 13, approved on 5 August 2024 and in force from 14 August 2025.
events.significance: An early non-European omnibus law that later won Israel an EU adequacy finding, and one that puts a general privacy right, a privacy tort and database regulation in a single statute.

sources.title: Data Protection Laws of the World — Israel
sources.quote: The laws that govern the right to privacy in Israel are the Basic Law: Human Dignity and Liberty, 5752 -1992; the Protection of Privacy Law, 5741-1981 and the regulations promulgated thereunder (the 'PPL') and the guidelines of the Israel Privacy Authority (as defined below).
sources.note: Law-firm global guide (secondary); used where the official gazette could not be read by script.

sources.title: Data Protection Laws of the World — Israel
sources.quote: On August 5, 2024, the Israel Knesset approved PPL (Amendment No. 13), 5774-2024 (" Amendment 13 ") which shall come into effect on August 14, 2025.
sources.note: Law-firm global guide (secondary); used where the official gazette could not be read by script.

sources.institution: WIPO Lex (unofficial English translation prepared by WIPO, 2014; Hebrew version controlling)
sources.title: Protection of Privacy Law, 5741-1981
sources.quote: An infringement of privacy constitutes a civil wrong, and the provisions of the Torts Ordinance [New Version] shall apply therein
sources.note: --check FOUND (s.4). The same text has s.5, 'a person who willfully infringes the privacy of another in any of the ways enumerated under sections 2(1), (3) to (7) and (9) to (11), shall be liable to five years imprisonment.' (FOUND), and the table of contents entry 'Chapter Two: Protection of Privacy in Databases' (FOUND). This is the consolidated text as amended to 2014.

sources.title: Charting its own path — The new reform in Israeli data protection laws
sources.quote: Soon after the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development published its first set of guidelines, Israel enacted the PPL. At that time, 43 years ago, it was one of the first global attempts to create a comprehensive statutory framework for privacy protection.
sources.note: --check FOUND. Supports 'one of the world's first' (replacing the unsourced 'first in the Middle East'). datePublished 2024-08-05 in the page metadata.

sources.title: Adequacy decisions
sources.quote: The European Commission has so far recognised: Andorra , Argentina , Brazil , Canada (commercial organisations), Faroe Islands , Guernsey , Israel , Isle of Man , Japan , Jersey , New Zealand , Republic of Korea , Switzerland ,
sources.note: --check FOUND. On this page 'Israel' links to CELEX 32011D0061 (Commission Decision 2011/61/EU of 31 January 2011). Supports the adequacy finding in the significance.

events.locationNote: Knesset building, Jerusalem. Day of enactment not verified; 5741 is the Hebrew calendar year (1980–81).

issues: 'It was the first data-protection statute in the Middle East' is an unsourced 'first'. Neither DLA Piper quote says it, and no source found says it either. The IAPP (Dan Or-Hof, 5 Aug 2024) describes the law as 'one of the first global attempts to create a comprehensive statutory framework for privacy protection', enacted soon after the OECD guidelines. The claim has been replaced with that.

The claim that the law combines a tort, criminal offences and database rules was not supported by either cited quote, which only name the law and Amendment 13. Added the WIPO Lex English translation. It shows s.4 (infringement of privacy is a civil wrong), s.5 (wilful infringement is an offence) and Chapter Two, 'Protection of Privacy in Databases' (registration under s.8). Note that WIPO's text is the 2014 consolidated version, so it includes later amendments; the 1981 law already had the Chapter One and Chapter Two structure.

Significance: 'one of the few to join a general privacy right with database regulation' is an unsourced comparative claim, so it has been reworded to describe what the statute does. The 'EU adequacy finding' (Decision 2011/61/EU) is supported by the Commission's adequacy page, which lists Israel. The archived EUR-Lex copy of 2011/61/EU could not be fetched because web.archive.org reset the connection.
Amendment 13 dates (approved 5 August 2024, in force 14 August 2025) are verbatim in DLA Piper. DLA Piper's '5774-2024' is its own Hebrew-year typo (it should be 5784). The record does not repeat it.

events.title: Chile enacts Latin America's first general data-protection statute
events.place: National Congress of Chile, Valparaíso
events.summary: Law No. 19.628 on the protection of private life, published in the Diario Oficial on 28 August 1999, regulated the processing of personal data in registers and databanks held by public bodies and private parties. It created no supervisory authority, so people had to go to the ordinary courts to enforce it. Law 21.719, published on 13 December 2024, rewrote it and created a Personal Data Protection Agency; the new regime takes full effect in December 2026.
events.significance: Began the shift in Latin America from constitutional habeas data to general statutes, though for a quarter of a century Chile's law had no regulator to enforce it.

sources.institution: Red Iberoamericana de Protección de Datos (RIPD)
sources.title: Ley N° 19.628 sobre protección de la vida privada
sources.quote: Ley N° 19.628, publicada el 28 de agosto de 1999, sobre protección de la vida privada
sources.note: Translation: 'Law No. 19.628, published on 28 August 1999, on the protection of private life'.

sources.title: Data Protection Laws of the World — Chile
sources.quote: The PDPL generally defines and regulates the processing of personal data in public and private databases and is thus the primary body of rules on the processing of personal data not governed by sectoral provisions (for example contained in the laws mentioned below).
sources.note: Law-firm global guide (secondary); used where the official gazette could not be read by script.

sources.title: Chile’s New Data Protection Law: Context, Overview, and Key Takeaways
sources.quote: The LPPD was introduced in the Senate in 2017 to replace Law 19.628 , Ley sobre Protección de la Vida Privada (hereinafter referred to as “LPVP”), which was adopted in 1999 as Chile’s first national data protection framework, as well as the first such law in Latin America.
sources.note: --check FOUND. Supports 'first in Latin America'. The same post says 'The legislation was published on December 13, 2024, and will become fully effective twenty-four months after that date (in December 2026).' (FOUND) and 'the LPPD creates, for the first time, a DPA vested with supervisory, regulatory, and sanctioning powers' (FOUND).

sources.institution: Derechos Digitales (Pablo Viollier), with funding from Privacy International
sources.title: El estado de la protección de datos personales en Chile
sources.quote: Una de las principales críticas respecto de la capacidad que tienen las personas naturales para hacer efectiva la observancia de los preceptos contenidos en la Ley 19.628 es la ausencia de una autoridad pública de control, como existe en otras latitudes. La ausencia de dicha autoridad de control implica que los individuos afectados deben recurrir ante los tribunales ordinarios de justicia
sources.note: --check FOUND (section 2.7.1). Translation: 'One of the main criticisms ... is the absence of a public supervisory authority, as exists elsewhere. The absence of such an authority means that affected individuals must go to the ordinary courts'. The report also calls 19.628 'una de las primeras leyes de protección de datos personales en América Latina' and notes that Ley 20.285 (2008) gave the Consejo para la Transparencia a limited, non-sanctioning oversight role over public bodies. Licensed CC BY 4.0.

sources.title: Publican la Ley N° 21.719 que modifica la Ley N° 19.628 sobre Protección de la Vida Privada en el Diario Oficial
sources.quote: Hoy, viernes 13 de diciembre de 2024, se publicó en el Diario Oficial la Ley N° 21.719, que modifica la Ley N° 19.628 sobre Protección de la Vida Privada.
sources.note: --check FOUND. Law-firm note (secondary).

sources.institution: Dirección de Presupuestos (DIPRES), Government of Chile
sources.title: Ley Nº 19.628 sobre protección de la vida privada o protección de datos de carácter personal
sources.quote: El tratamiento de los datos de carácter personal en registros o bancos de datos por organismos públicos o por particulares se sujetará a las disposiciones de esta ley
sources.note: --check FOUND (Art. 1). The header reads '(Publicada en el Diario Oficial de 28 de agosto de 1999)' (FOUND).

events.locationNote: Chile's National Congress sits in Valparaíso. 'First in Latin America' refers to general statutes; Brazil (1988) and Argentina (1994) had constitutional habeas data earlier.

issues: Unsourced claims. Neither cited quote supports 'first in Latin America', 'created no supervisory authority, so enforcement fell to the courts' or the December 2024 Law 21.719. Added FPF (Maria Badillo, 27 Feb 2025), which says the law was 'the first such law in Latin America' and that Law 21.719 creates a DPA 'for the first time' and was published on 13 December 2024. Added Derechos Digitales (Pablo Viollier, Feb 2017), which says the absence of a supervisory authority means people had to go to the ordinary courts. Added Carey (13 Dec 2024) for the Diario Oficial publication. Also added the law text (DIPRES copy) for the public and private scope.
Title says 'passes' while displayDate is the Diario Oficial publication date (28 August 1999). Changed to 'enacts' so the verb does not assert the date Congress voted.

'Set up a Personal Data Protection Agency' suggested the agency is already running. Law 21.719 becomes fully effective only in December 2026 (FPF; DLA Piper: 'effective December 1, 2026'), which has not yet happened as of 2026-09-23. Reworded. For the same reason the significance line 'for 25 years without a regulator' has been reworded.

Confirmed: published on 28 August 1999 (RIPD; the DIPRES text reads '(Publicada en el Diario Oficial de 28 de agosto de 1999)'); scope 'por organismos públicos o por particulares' (Art. 1); coordinates of the National Congress in Valparaíso.

events.title: Cabo Verde enacts Africa's first data-protection law
events.place: Assembleia Nacional, Praia, Cabo Verde
events.summary: Law No. 133/V/2001, approved by the National Assembly on 20 December 2000 and dated 22 January 2001, made Cabo Verde the first African country to enact comprehensive data-protection legislation. It closely followed European law, as Cabo Verde's legal system draws on Portugal's, and it put into effect Article 44 of the Constitution, which already gave citizens the right of access to computerised data about them and to have it corrected. Amended in 2013 and 2021, the law was later backed by a national data-protection commission (CNPD).
events.significance: Opened the African chapter of the omnibus model, a decade before regional harmonisation began.

sources.title: Cabo Verde — Fact Sheet
sources.quote: Law No. 133-V-2001 , passed in 2001, was Cabo Verde’s original data protection law, and make Cabo Verde the first African country to have enacted comprehensive data protection legislation.

sources.title: Data Protection Laws of the World — Cape Verde
sources.quote: Data Protection Law (Law 133/V/2001 (as amended by Law 41/VIII/2013, Law 121/IX/2021 of 17 March 2021) and Law 132/V/2001, of 22 January 2001.
sources.note: Law-firm global guide (secondary); used where the official gazette could not be read by script.

sources.institution: Boletim Oficial da República de Cabo Verde, text hosted by AFAPDP (Association francophone des autorités de protection des données personnelles)
sources.title: Lei nº 133/V/2001, de 22 de Janeiro — Regime jurídico geral de protecção de dados pessoais a pessoas singulares
sources.quote: Aprovada em 20 de Dezembro de 2000.
sources.note: --check FOUND. The same text has 'Promulgada em 10 de Janeiro de 2001.' (FOUND), and its preamble says the Constitution establishes (Art. 44 no. 1) that todos «os cidadãos têm direitos de acesso aos dados informatizados que lhes digam respeito (FOUND), 'podendo exigir a sua rectificação e actualização'. The PDF's 'fi' ligature blocks --check on the rest of that sentence.

events.locationNote: National Assembly building, Achada Santo António, Praia.

issues: Title and date are off. The law's own text says 'Aprovada em 20 de Dezembro de 2000' (National Assembly approval), 'Promulgada em 10 de Janeiro de 2001', and it is designated 'Lei nº 133/V/2001, de 22 de Janeiro'. So the Assembly passed it in December 2000 and the law is dated 22 January 2001. The title 'passes ... 2001' has been changed to 'enacts', and displayDate made precise (year 2001 unchanged).

'The Constitution already gave citizens a habeas data remedy': none of the cited sources dates the habeas data provision. Data Protection Africa describes today's constitution, and the habeas data procedure law it mentions is Law 109/IV/94. The law's own preamble instead cites Article 44 of the Constitution, which gives citizens the right of access to computerised data about them and to have it corrected. That verifiable provision replaces the sentence.

Coordinates (14.931, -23.5125) are about 2.8 km north of the National Assembly building. The building is in Achada Santo António, Praia, at 14.9061, -23.5154 (Wikipedia 'National Assembly (Cape Verde)').

Confirmed: 'first African country to have enacted comprehensive data protection legislation' (Data Protection Africa), the Portuguese/European model, and the 2013 and 2021 amendments (DLA Piper: Law 41/VIII/2013 and Law 121/IX/2021 of 17 March 2021). A national commission (CNPD) was created under Law 42/VIII/2013. The original law had entrusted oversight to a parliamentary commission ('A fiscalização da protecção de dados pessoais é assegurada pela Assembleia Nacional').

events.title: West African leaders bind their states to adopt data-protection laws
events.place: 37th Session of the ECOWAS Authority of Heads of State and Government, Abuja, Nigeria
events.summary: Meeting in Abuja on 16 February 2010, ECOWAS heads of state signed Supplementary Act A/SA.1/01/10 on Personal Data Protection. It requires each member state to establish a legal framework for data protection and its own independent data-protection authority.
events.significance: Made regional harmonisation the African route: binding community law first, national laws after.

sources.title: Supplementary Act A/SA.1/01/10 on Personal Data Protection within ECOWAS
sources.quote: HAVE SIGNED THIS SUPPLEMENTARY ACT DONE AT ABUJA ON 16TH DAYOF FEBRUARY 2010 IN A SINGLE ORIGINAL IN ENGLISH, FRENCH AND PORTUGUESE
sources.note: OCR text layer of a scanned original.

sources.title: Supplementary Act A/SA.1/01/10 — Article 14
sources.quote: Within the ECOWAS space, each Member State shall establish Its own data protection Authority.
sources.note: OCR text layer ('Its' as printed in the OCR).

events.locationNote: Abuja city coordinates; the summit venue is not named in the Act.

issues: No errors found. Re-fetched the Statewatch copy; both quotes FOUND in the OCR layer. The header reads 'THIRTY-SEVENTH SESSION OF THE AUTHORITY OF HEADS OF STATE AND GOVERNMENT' and ''Ahuja' [OCR for Abuja], 16th February 2010'. Article 2 requires 'Each Member State shall establish a legal framework of protection for privacy of data'. Article 14 requires a national data protection authority, and the Act says that authority 'Shall be an independent administrative authority'. Abuja coordinates are correct.

events.title: Uruguay becomes the first non-European state to join Convention 108
events.place: Council of Europe, Strasbourg, France (deposit of accession)
events.summary: In 2013 Uruguay became the first non-European state to accede to the Council of Europe's data-protection Convention 108 and its Additional Protocol: its accession, approved by law in December 2012, was completed in April 2013 and took effect on 1 August 2013, making it the Convention's 45th party. By 2019 seven more non-European states had followed: Mauritius, Senegal, Tunisia, Cabo Verde, Mexico, Argentina and Morocco. Uruguay approved the modernised 'Convention 108+' in 2021, after Mauritius had ratified it in 2020.
events.significance: Made Convention 108, open to non-European states since 1981 but joined by none until then, the first data-protection treaty with parties outside Europe: the only binding international standard with the potential to apply worldwide.

sources.title: Uruguay es el primer país no europeo en adherir al Convenio 108+ sobre protección de datos personales
sources.quote: Tal como sucedió en 2013 con la aprobación del Convenio del Consejo de Europa para la protección de las personas con respecto al tratamiento automatizado de datos, Uruguay acaba de aprobar la modernización de Convenio transformándose nuevamente en el primero país no europeo en hacerlo.
sources.note: Translation: 'As happened in 2013 with the approval of the Council of Europe Convention..., Uruguay has just approved the modernisation of the Convention, once again becoming the first non-European country to do so.' Uruguay's approving law (Ley 19.030) and the 2013 deposit date were not read at the primary; the Council of Europe treaty office blocks scripts. Verification: Quote re-fetched and FOUND, but the claim it makes about 108+ is false: Mauritius ratified the amending Protocol CETS 223 on 4 September 2020, before Uruguay's approving law of 16 April 2021. Its 2013 claim is also loose, since the approving law (Ley 19.030) dates from 23 December 2012 and only the accession fell in 2013. Superseded by the URCDP and PL&B sources added below; do not cite for '108+ first'.

sources.institution: Instituto Nacional de Transparencia, Acceso a la Información y Protección de Datos Personales (INAI), Mexico
sources.title: El Convenio 108 y el Comité Consultivo
sources.quote: Fuera de la región europea, han suscrito el Convenio 108 y su Protocolo adicional Uruguay, Mauricio, Senegal, Túnez, Cabo Verde, México, Argentina y Marruecos.
sources.note: Translation: 'Outside the European region, Uruguay, Mauritius, Senegal, Tunisia, Cabo Verde, Mexico, Argentina and Morocco have subscribed to Convention 108 and its Additional Protocol.'

sources.institution: Unidad Reguladora y de Control de Datos Personales (URCDP), Uruguay
sources.title: Uruguay ratificó la Convención 108 modernizada
sources.quote: En el 2013, Uruguay se constituyó como el primer país no europeo miembro del Convenio 108 del Consejo de Europa y su Protocolo Adicional de 2001, el que fue aprobado por Ley N° 19.030 , el 23 de diciembre de 2012.
sources.note: Translation: 'In 2013 Uruguay became the first non-European member of Council of Europe Convention 108 and its 2001 Additional Protocol, which was approved by Law No. 19.030 of 23 December 2012.' The same page says the 108+ ratification followed parliamentary approval by Ley 19.948 of 16 April 2021. Page date 16/06/2021 from the HTML.

sources.title: Uruguay's accession to CoE DP Convention paves way for it to become a wider international treaty
sources.quote: On 12 April 2013 the Council of Europe announced that Uruguay's accession to Convention 108 (and to its Additional Protocol) was complete. It will enter into force regarding Uruguay on 1 August 2013, making it the 45th state to become a party, and the first non-European party, to the Convention.
sources.note: Independent report of the Council of Europe announcement; the CoE's own pages return HTTP 403 to scripts.

sources.title: Communiqué: Ratification of the Protocol amending Convention 108 (CETS 223) by Mauritius
sources.quote: We have the pleasure to inform you that Mauritius has signed and deposited, on 4 September 2020, its instrument of ratification of the Protocol amending Convention for the Protection of individuals with regard to automatic processing of personal data (CETS 223).
sources.note: Shows that a non-European state ratified 108+ before Uruguay. The same communiqué: 'Mauritius has thus become the 6th State after Bulgaria, Croatia, Lithuania, Poland and Serbia as well as the first country in Africa to ratify the modernised Convention 108 (Convention 108 +).' (FOUND)

events.locationNote: Accessions are deposited with the Council of Europe in Strasbourg (Palais de l'Europe).

issues: False claim: 'in 2021 the first to approve the modernised Convention 108+'. Mauritius signed and deposited its ratification of the amending Protocol (CETS 223) on 4 September 2020, as the 6th state overall and the first in Africa. Uruguay's approving law (Ley 19.948) is dated 16 April 2021. Uruguay was therefore not the first non-European state to approve 108+. The Ferrere source's claim that it was ('nuevamente en el primero país no europeo en hacerlo') is wrong on this point.

'Adopt' is imprecise. Uruguay's parliament approved Convention 108 and the Additional Protocol by Ley 19.030 of 23 December 2012 (URCDP). The Council of Europe announced the accession complete on 12 April 2013, and it entered into force for Uruguay on 1 August 2013, as the 45th party and the first non-European one.
Significance overstates. Convention 108 was open to accession by non-member states from 1981; Uruguay was the first to take that up, it did not 'turn' the treaty into one open to the world.
'By around 2019': Morocco, the last of the seven, deposited in May 2019, so 'By 2019' is accurate. The seven names match the INAI list.

The Ferrere quote is verbatim (FOUND) but should not stand as support because of the false 108+ claim. It is replaced by the regulator's own statement (URCDP) and the PL&B report of the Council of Europe announcement.

events.title: The Council of Europe opens 'Convention 108+' for signature
events.place: Council of Europe, Palais de l'Europe, Strasbourg, France
events.summary: The protocol modernising Convention 108 (CETS No. 223), known as Convention 108+, was adopted by the Council of Europe's Committee of Ministers on 18 May 2018 and opened for signature in Strasbourg in October 2018, updating the 1981 treaty for the GDPR era. Ratification has been slow: Slovakia's, deposited on 15 June 2023, was the 25th. The first state outside Europe to ratify was Mauritius, which deposited its ratification on 4 September 2020 as the sixth state overall.
events.significance: The only candidate for a binding global privacy treaty; its slow ratification shows how hard it is to make privacy rules universal by treaty.

sources.title: Uruguay es el primer país no europeo en adherir al Convenio 108+ sobre protección de datos personales
sources.quote: El Parlamento acaba de aprobar el “Protocolo de enmienda del Convenio para la Protección de las Personas con respecto al Tratamiento de Datos Personales” suscrito en Estrasburgo en octubre de 2018, conocido como Convenio 108+, manteniendo de esta manera al país a la vanguardia en regulación de datos personales.
sources.note: Translation: 'Parliament has just approved the Protocol amending the Convention..., signed in Strasbourg in October 2018, known as Convention 108+'. Used only for the October 2018 signing in Strasbourg. The article's headline claim that Uruguay was the first non-European country to adhere to Convention 108+ is wrong: Mauritius ratified on 4 September 2020. The exact opening date (10 October 2018) could not be read on coe.int, which blocks scripts.

sources.institution: Úrad na ochranu osobných údajov (Office for Personal Data Protection of the Slovak Republic)
sources.title: Ratification and deposit of instruments of ratification of the CETS 223 protocol
sources.quote: The Slovak Republic is the 25th country that ratified the CETS 223 protocol.

sources.institution: Data Protection Office, Republic of Mauritius
sources.title: Communiqué — Ratification of the Protocol amending Convention for the Protection of individuals with regard to automatic processing of personal data (CETS 223) by Mauritius
sources.quote: Mauritius has thus become the 6th State after Bulgaria, Croatia, Lithuania, Poland and Serbia as well as the first country in Africa to ratify the modernised Convention 108 (Convention 108 +).
sources.note: The preceding sentence, also FOUND, reads: 'Mauritius has signed and deposited, on 4 September 2020, its instrument of ratification of the Protocol amending Convention for the Protection of individuals with regard to automatic processing of personal data (CETS 223).'

sources.institution: Council of Europe (copy hosted by the European Parliament, LIBE committee)
sources.title: Convention 108 + — Convention for the protection of individuals with regard to the processing of personal data
sources.quote: The Protocol was adopted by the Committee of Ministers on 18 May 2018.
sources.note: Council of Europe booklet, '© Council of Europe, June 2018'. --check FOUND.

events.locationNote: Palais de l'Europe, Strasbourg.

issues: False claim: 'Uruguay was the first non-European state to approve it, in 2021.' Mauritius signed and deposited its instrument of ratification of CETS 223 on 4 September 2020, becoming 'the 6th State after Bulgaria, Croatia, Lithuania, Poland and Serbia as well as the first country in Africa' to ratify (Data Protection Office of Mauritius communiqué, FOUND). All five earlier ratifiers are European, so Mauritius, not Uruguay, was the first state outside Europe. Uruguay's parliament approved the protocol only in April 2021. The Ferrere headline repeats the error, probably carried over from Uruguay being the first non-European state to accede to the original Convention 108 (2013), which the article's first paragraph mentions.
The Ferrere quote is verbatim and still supports 'signed in Strasbourg in October 2018', so it is kept for that fact only. Its note is corrected.

events.title: Sri Lanka passes a dedicated personal-data protection law
events.place: Parliament of Sri Lanka, Sri Jayawardenepura Kotte
events.summary: Sri Lanka's Parliament passed the Personal Data Protection Bill with amendments on 9 March 2022, and the Speaker certified it on 19 March as the Personal Data Protection Act No. 9 of 2022. The country's Data Protection Authority describes it as the first independent personal-data legislation in South Asia; Nepal's broader Individual Privacy Act of 2018 also covers personal information. The Act was amended by Act No. 22 of 2025.
events.significance: Opened South Asia, home to about a quarter of humanity, to the omnibus model, ahead of India (2023) and Bangladesh (2025).

events.title: India enacts the Digital Personal Data Protection Act
events.place: Parliament House, New Delhi, India
events.summary: Six years after the Supreme Court recognised privacy as a fundamental right, India enacted the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023), published on 11 August 2023. Until then India had no standalone data-protection law and relied on the Information Technology Act 2000 and rules made in 2011. The Act's provisions take effect on dates the central government notifies.
events.significance: Brought the world's most populous country, and its large digital-identity and payments systems, under a consent-centred data law.

events.title: A global census counts 172 countries with data-privacy laws
events.place: Privacy Laws & Business, Pinner, north-west London (publisher); author at Macquarie Law School, Sydney
events.summary: Graham Greenleaf's running census of national data-privacy laws, published in Privacy Laws & Business International Report, counted 172 countries with such laws as at 15 March 2025. That is an average of 3.3 new countries a year since Sweden's 1973 law, rising to 5.4 a year since 2020. His April 2025 biennial assessment, the ninth since 2011, concluded for the first time that revising existing laws now mattered more than enacting new ones. A year-by-year list of all 172 followed in June 2025.
events.significance: Shows that the argument has moved from whether to have a privacy law to what kind, which is the space where machine-readable, person-proffered terms now compete.

Since 2020 the average number of new laws per year has risen to 5.4.

laws.law: Datalag (1973:289) — Data Act
laws.note: The world's first national data-protection statute. It created the Datainspektionen (Data Inspection Board, today IMY), which licensed personal-data registers. It followed the German state of Hesse's 1970 law, which was sub-national.

Samtidigt trädde reglerna i datalagen om tillsyn över personregister i kraft. De bestämmelser som avser tillståndsfrågor trädde i kraft först ett år senare då grundlagsändring skett.

At the same time the Data Act's rules on supervision of personal registers came into force. The provisions on permits came into force only a year later, once a constitutional amendment had been made.' The line-break hyphen in 'datainspek tionen' is as printed on the digitised page.

The next sentences say the applicant is the controller and 'Kravet på tillstånd gäller både myndigheter och företag eller andra' (the permit requirement applies to authorities and companies alike). --check FOUND.

issues: Both quotes were re-fetched and found word for word. data.riksdagen.se gives 'Utfärdad: 1973-05-11' and 'Upphävd: 1998-10-24'. Jan Freese's 1979 SvJT article dates the Data Inspection Board and the supervision rules to 1 July 1973 and the permit rules to a year later, so inForce 1973 holds for the first provisions.

Minor wording point, not changed: under the original 1973 Act the Board granted a permit ('tillstånd') for every computerised personal register, public or private. The separate 'licens' came only with Lag 1982:446. 'Licensed' is fine as plain English. Freese's description of the permit requirement is added as a source.
The 'world's first national' claim is backed by Greenleaf ('since 1973 when Sweden enacted the first national data privacy law'). The coordinates match the Riksdag in Stockholm.
