laws.law: Bundesdatenschutzgesetz (BDSG) — Federal Data Protection Act
laws.regulator: Bundesbeauftragter für den Datenschutz (BfD; since 2006 the Bundesbeauftragte für den Datenschutz und die Informationsfreiheit, BfDI)
laws.note: The first federal data-protection act. It was signed in Bonn on 27 January 1977 by President Walter Scheel and promulgated in the Federal Law Gazette on 1 February 1977 (BGBl. I S. 201). Most of it took effect on 1 January 1978. The sections providing for a Federal Commissioner for Data Protection (§§ 17–18) took effect earlier, on 1 July 1977, and the first commissioner, Hans Peter Bull, took office on 14 February 1978. Hesse's Data Protection Act, dated 7 October 1970 and in force from 13 October 1970, had been the world's first data-protection law.

The page also says processing was allowed only with consent or where the BDSG or another legal provision allowed it, that it was meant to stop 'staatliche Stellen, aber auch Unternehmen' helping themselves to personal data, and: 'Der erste Verantwortliche für diese Aufgabe war der Rechtswissenschaftler Hans Peter Bull, der am 14. Februar 1978 in sein Amt eingeführt wurde.' The page's section heading reads '28. Januar 1977' while its text says 27 January; the statute is dated 27 January 1977 (BGBl. I 1977 S. 201).

sources.note: Gives the official citation (Act of 7 October 1970, GVBl. 1970 Nr. 41 S. 625) and says 'Das Datenschutzgesetz des Landes Hessen trat am 13. Oktober 1970 in Kraft'. The linked gazette scan (starweb.hessen.de/cache/GVBL/1970/00041.pdf) downloads, but it is an image-only PDF with no text layer, so it could not be checked for the quote. issues: 'Adopted 27 January 1977 while the Bundestag sat in Bonn' confuses the Act's date with a parliamentary vote. 27 January 1977 is the date of signature ('Das vorstehende Gesetz wird hiermit ausgefertigt ... Bonn, den 27. Januar 1977', signed by President Scheel). The gazette, BGBl. I Nr. 7, was issued on 1 February 1977. The Bundestag's votes came earlier, in 1976. The BfDI page's 'verabschiedet am 27. Januar 1977' is loose usage, and the BfDI page even heads the entry '28. Januar 1977'.

'It took effect on 1 January 1978, which is also when the post of Federal Data Protection Commissioner was created' is contradicted by the statute. § 47 BDSG 1977 reads: 'Dieses Gesetz tritt am 1. Januar 1978 in Kraft. Abweichend davon treten in Kraft: ... 2. §§ 17, 18, 28 und 38 am 1. Juli 1977'. § 17 is headed 'Bestellung eines Bundesbeauftragten für den Datenschutz'. So the provisions creating the post took effect on 1 July 1977. The BfDI's own milestone of 1 January 1978 simplifies this. The first commissioner, Hans Peter Bull, took office on 14 February 1978.

Hesse: 'had passed the world's first data-protection law on 7 October 1970' is shaky. 7 October 1970 is the Act's official date (GVBl. I S. 625). The BfDI page cited as source 0 gives 30 September 1970 ('Hessen erlässt ...') and entry into force on 13 October 1970. Secondary sources disagree about the day the Landtag voted, so the wording now avoids 'passed on'.
Regulator label: in 1977 the office was the Bundesbeauftragter für den Datenschutz (BfD). The 'und die Informationsfreiheit' (BfDI) name dates from 2006.

sources.quote: Datatilsynet er et norsk, uavhengig forvaltningsorgan administrativt underordnet Digitaliserings- og forvaltningsdepartementet , opprettet 1. januar 1980.
sources.note: Translation: 'Datatilsynet is a Norwegian independent administrative body ... established 1 January 1980.' The page lists Helge Seip as the first director (1980–1989). Tertiary source; it agrees with Føyen. --check FOUND.

issues: 'Passed by the Storting on 9 June 1978' is probably a conflation, though the cited article says so word for word. 9 June 1978 is the Act's official date (LOV-1978-06-09-48). Norwegian Acts of that era are dated by royal sanction in the Council of State, which met on Fridays. 9 June 1978 was a Friday, and other Acts share the date, such as the Equality Act, LOV-1978-06-09-45. The Odelsting and Lagting votes normally came earlier. The actual vote dates could not be found (lovdata.no returns HTTP 405 to scripts), so the note now gives the Act's official date without claiming a Storting vote on that day.

Missing context: the Act and its regulations took effect on 1 January 1980, and the Datatilsynet was set up on that date. Sources: Føyen, 'iverksettes sammen med loven pr. 1. januar 1980'; SNL, 'Trådt i kraft 01.01.1980, 01.07.1980'; no.wikipedia, 'opprettet 1. januar 1980'.
Source 1 (Paperjam) is dated '2026'. The article's datePublished is 2005-01-21, as the lu-1979 record already has it.
Checked and correct: law name, regulator, Oslo coordinates (Storting). The Paperjam list (Norway among the 1978 laws) is a weak secondary source that the law's year does not depend on.

laws.law: Lov nr. 293 om private registre m.v. and Lov nr. 294 om offentlige myndigheders registre, both of 8 June 1978 (Private Registers Act and Public Authorities' Registers Act)
laws.note: Denmark regulated personal-data registers in two Acts of 8 June 1978, one for the private sector (No. 293) and one for public authorities (No. 294). Both were overseen by the Registertilsynet, which the Datatilsynet replaced under the 2000 Act on Processing of Personal Data.

sources.quote: A l'époque, le Grand-Duché faisait même partie des pionniers, puisque seuls sept autres pays avaient précédemment légiféré dans ce domaine: la Suède, dès 1973, puis l'Allemagne et le Canada (en 1977), la France, la Norvège et le Danemark et enfin l'Autriche (en 1978).
sources.note: Translation: 'At the time the Grand Duchy was even among the pioneers, since only seven other countries had legislated in this field: Sweden from 1973, then Germany and Canada (in 1977), France, Norway and Denmark and finally Austria (in 1978).' Canada's 1977 entry refers to privacy provisions in Part IV of the Canadian Human Rights Act; see the Canada record.

(Registerlov)' and Lov nr. 294 'Lov om offentlige myndigheders registre', both signed 1978-06-08 (DiesSigni) and published in Lovtidende A by the Justitsministeriet. Regulator confirmed by Den Store Danske/lex.dk: 'Registertilsynet var et organ, der tilså, at registerlovene blev overholdt. Efter 2000 afløst af Datatilsynet.' (da.wikipedia says the name lasted to 2002, so the note gives no exact year.)
The note's statement that only a secondary source was read, because the portal is script-rendered, is out of date now that the primary metadata has been read.
Source 0 (Paperjam) is dated '2026'. The article's datePublished is 2005-01-21.

laws.note: Required prior ministerial authorisation to create or run a databank of personal data.

sources.note: The same page: 'La loi a subi des modifications importantes en 1992' and the 2002 law 'avait abrogé l'ancienne loi sur la protection des données de 1979.'

sources.title: Protection de la vie privée: une culture à établir
sources.quote: Ce texte de 1979 prévoyait de soumettre toute création et toute exploitation d'une banque de données nominatives à une autorisation préalable du ministre de la Justice, sur avis d'une commission consultative qui examinait individuellement les demandes d'autorisation introduites.
sources.note: Translation: 'This 1979 text required every creation and operation of a personal data bank to have prior authorisation from the Minister of Justice, on the opinion of a consultative commission that examined each application individually.' The Legilux gazette page is script-rendered and was not read.

issues: Both quotes were re-fetched and found word for word. The CNPD page gives the official title, says the Act was substantially amended in 1992 and was repealed by the 2002 law. Paperjam, dated correctly at 2005-01-21 per its JSON-LD datePublished, supports prior authorisation by the Minister of Justice on the opinion of a consultative commission.

The law title and 31 March 1979 date are confirmed. The coordinates are Luxembourg City (Chamber of Deputies). The missing regulator field is reasonable: the 1979 Act used ministerial authorisation plus a consultative commission, and the CNPD came only in 2002.
The Legilux gazette page (legilux.public.lu/eli/etat/leg/loi/1979/03/31/n1/jo, including the /fr/pdf and /fr/html forms) is script-rendered and could not be read. No primary text was checked.

issues: Both quotes were re-fetched and found word for word. The long title and '[12th July 1984]' (the date of Royal Assent) are on legislation.gov.uk's as-enacted text. The ICO page gives the ten-person Registrar's office in 1984 and the photo caption 'Eric Howe CBE, Data Protection Registrar 1984-1994'.

The claims that it 'created a Data Protection Registrar' and 'covered only automatically processed information' are both correct. Section 3(1)(a) of the Act as enacted creates 'an officer known as the Data Protection Registrar'. That text is added as a direct statutory source. The coordinates match the Palace of Westminster.

laws.law: Henkilörekisterilaki (471/1987) — Personal Data File Act
laws.note: Finland's first general law on personal data files, given on 30 April 1987 and in force from 1 January 1988, with the Data Protection Ombudsman (tietosuojavaltuutettu) as supervisor. It was repealed in 1999 by the Personal Data Act (523/1999), which brought Finnish law into line with the EU Data Protection Directive.

sources.note: Translation: 'The Data Protection Ombudsman supervises the collection, storage, use and disclosure of personal data to achieve the aims of this Act.' The office itself was set up by the companion Act 474/1987, which the same statute cites.

sources.note: Translation: 'This Act repeals the Personal Data File Act (471/1987) given on 30 April 1987, together with its later amendments.' The Personal Data Act was signed in Helsinki on 22 April 1999 and entered into force on 1 June 1999 (both on the same page).

sources.title: HE 96/1998 Hallituksen esitys Eduskunnalle henkilötietolaiksi ja eräiksi siihen liittyviksi laeiksi
sources.quote: Esityksessä ehdotetaan säädettäväksi henkilötietolaki, joka korvaisi vuoden 1987 henkilörekisterilain. Esityksellä saatetaan voimassa oleva henkilötietojen keräämistä, tallettamista, käyttöä ja luovuttamista koskeva yleislainsäädäntö vastaamaan yksilöiden suojelusta henkilötietojen käsittelyssä ja näiden tietojen vapaasta liikkuvuudesta annettua Euroopan parlamentin ja neuvoston direktiiviä
sources.note: Government bill. Translation: 'The bill proposes a Personal Data Act to replace the 1987 Personal Data File Act. It brings the current general legislation on the collection, storage, use and disclosure of personal data into line with the Directive of the European Parliament and of the Council on the protection of individuals with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data'. That is Directive 95/46/EC.

issues: The only source's quote is the Finlex page title ('Henkilörekisterilaki | 471/1987 | Suomen säädöskokoelma'). It supports the name, the number and the year and nothing more. The finlex.fi page renders the statute text by script, so the fetched page is only a title and menu. The note's claims about the supervising Data Protection Ombudsman and about replacement in 1999 by a Personal Data Act implementing the EU Directive had no source.

All the claims are correct. The original statute text in Finlex's open-data service gives the signing line 'Helsingissä 30 päivänä huhtikuuta 1987' and entry into force on 1 January 1988, and it makes the tietosuojavaltuutettu the supervisor. The Personal Data Act 523/1999 expressly repeals 471/1987. The government bill HE 96/1998 says the new act would replace the 1987 law and align it with the EU Data Protection Directive. Primary sources for each were added, and the note now gives the exact dates.
The coordinates (60.1725, 24.9335) are Parliament House in Helsinki, which is correct.

laws.law: Data Protection Act, 1988 (No. 25 of 1988)
laws.regulator: Data Protection Commissioner (now Data Protection Commission)
laws.note: Enacted on 13 July 1988 expressly to give effect to Council of Europe Convention 108, and created the Data Protection Commissioner (today the Data Protection Commission).

sources.note: Section 9(1) of the Act as enacted, which creates the office of Data Protection Commissioner.

issues: No errors found. The long title, quoted verbatim (FOUND), gives effect to Convention 108. The page carries the date '[13 th July , 1988]', and the Act is Number 25 of 1988.

The claim that the Act created the Data Protection Commissioner rests on the page's table of contents ('The Data Protection Commissioner 9. The Commissioner.'), not on the quote. Section 9's own wording was added as a supporting source. 'Today the Data Protection Commission' is correct: section 10 of the Data Protection Act 2018 establishes 'An Coimisiún um Chosaint Sonraí or, in the English language, the Data Protection Commission'.
The coordinates (53.3409, -6.254) are Leinster House, which is fine.

laws.note: A Czechoslovak federal act of 29 April 1992, in force 1 June 1992 and repealed on 1 June 2000 by Act 101/2000, which created the Czech Office for Personal Data Protection.

issues: No factual error. Re-fetched and FOUND on the page: 'ze dne 29. dubna 1992' [of 29 April 1992], 'Federální shromáždění České a Slovenské Federativní Republiky se usneslo' [the Federal Assembly of the ČSFR resolved], 'Platnost od 01.06.1992 Účinnost od 01.06.1992' [valid from, effective from] and 'Zrušeno k 01.06.2000 ( 101/2000 Sb. )' [repealed as of].

Unsupported claim: nothing sourced the statement that Act 101/2000 'created the Czech Office for Personal Data Protection'. Act 101/2000 Sb. was added. Its text says 'Zřizuje se Úřad pro ochranu osobních údajů' [the Office for Personal Data Protection is established] and expressly repeals 256/1992. It is dated 4 April 2000 and effective from 1 June 2000.
Minor: the coordinates (50.0875, 14.4213) are Old Town Square, a generic Prague point. The Federal Assembly sat about 1 km away on Vinohradská. This is acceptable at map scale, so no change was made.

The quote supports only the title. The claims that the law created the data-protection agency and was replaced in 1999 are on the same BOE page but were not quoted, so both lines were added as sources: '1. Se crea la Agencia de Protección de Datos.' and 'SE DEROGA, por Ley Orgánica 15/1999, de 13 de diciembre'. Publication in BOE núm. 262 on 31 October 1992 matches the source's date field.
The coordinates (40.4163, -3.6966) are the Congreso de los Diputados, which is fine.

laws.note: Dated 19 June 1992 and in force from 1 July 1993; covered federal bodies and private persons. Replaced by a revised FADP in force from 1 September 2023.

sources.quote: 1 Dieses Gesetz gilt für das Bearbeiten von Daten natürlicher und juristischer Personen durch: a. private Personen; b. Bundesorgane.
sources.note: Art. 2(1). Translation: 'This Act applies to the processing of data of natural and legal persons by: a. private persons; b. federal bodies.'

issues: No factual error, but two claims had no source. The Federal Office of Justice page supports the date of 19 June 1992 (the quote is FOUND) and the revised law's entry into force on 1 September 2023 ('Es ist am 1. September 2023 in Kraft getreten.', FOUND). It says nothing about entry into force in 1993 or about the law's scope, and the source note itself admits the 1993 date was not verified.

Fedlex (SR 235.1, version of 1 March 2019) was added. It shows 'Datum des Inkrafttretens: 1. Juli 1993' and Art. 2(1), under which the Act applies to processing by 'a. private Personen; b. Bundesorgane', which confirms 'federal bodies and private persons'. The note was sharpened to give the exact date of 1 July 1993.

Regulator: under the 1992 Act the office was the Eidgenössischer Datenschutzbeauftragter. It took the name EDÖB when the Transparency Act came in (2006). Giving the current name, as the other records do, is acceptable.

issues: The note's second clause ('the Garante ... publishes it as part of its founding legislation') is vague and is not what the page says. Rewritten with facts from the same page: published in the Gazzetta Ufficiale n. 5 on 8 January 1997, in force 120 days after publication (Art. 45), and repealed under Art. 183 of the Personal Data Protection Code (2003).

'Italy's first general data-protection law' matches the standard account. Italy had only sectoral rules before 1996, and the page does not contradict it. The coordinates (Montecitorio, Rome) are fine.

sources.title: ব্যক্তিগত উপাত্ত সুরক্ষা আইন, ২০২৬ (Personal Data Protection Act, 2026)
sources.quote: (৩) ধারা ২৩ এবং ধারা ৩১ হইতে ৩৫ ব্যতীত, এই আইন ৬ নভেম্বর, ২০২৫ তারিখে কার্যকর হইয়াছে বলিয়া গণ্য হইবে, এবং আইনটি জারির পরবর্তী ১৮ (আঠারো) মাস অতিবাহিত হইবার পর, সরকার, সরকারি গেজেটে প্রজ্ঞাপন দ্বারা, যে তারিখ নির্ধারণ করিবে সেই তারিখে উক্ত ধারাসমূহ কার্যকর হইবে।
sources.note: Section 1(3) of Act No. 63 of 2026 (header: '( ২০২৬ সনের ৬৩ নং আইন ) [ ১০ এপ্রিল, ২০২৬ ]'). Translation: 'Except section 23 and sections 31 to 35, this Act shall be deemed to have come into effect on 6 November 2025, and those sections shall come into effect on the date the Government fixes by notification in the official Gazette after 18 (eighteen) months have passed since the law was issued.' Section 44(1) on the same page repeals Ordinance No. 61 of 2025 and Ordinance No. 23 of 2026. Checked with fetch-text --check: FOUND.

sources.title: Parliament passes 31 bills related to IG-era ordinances
sources.quote: The remaining bills passed in the House are Bangladesh Building Regulatory Authority Bill, 2026; Rajdhani Unnaya Kartripakkha (RAJUK) Bill, 2026; Personal Data Protection Bill, 2026; Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation (Amendment) Bill, 2026 and Negotiable Instruments (Amendment) Bill, 2026.
sources.note: UNB wire report published 9 April 2026 ('Parliament passed a total of 31 bills on Thursday ... bidding to adopt, repeal or amend ordinances promulgated during the tenure of the interim government'). Checked with fetch-text --check: FOUND.

issues: The note says the ordinance's status after the elected parliament returned 'was not verified'. It has since been settled. On Thursday 9 April 2026 Parliament passed the Personal Data Protection Bill, 2026 as one of 31 bills dealing with interim-government ordinances (UNB/Financial Express). The official Laws of Bangladesh site lists the Personal Data Protection Act, 2026 as Act No. 63 of 2026, dated 10 April 2026. Section 44(1) of that Act repeals Ordinance No. 61 of 2025 and the amending Ordinance No. 23 of 2026. Under s.1(3) the Act is deemed in force from 6 November 2025, except s.23 and ss.31–35, which start on a date the government gazettes once 18 months have passed. The Laws of Bangladesh page for the ordinance says it 'has been repealed by the Personal Data Protection Act, 2026 (Act No. 63 of 2026)'.

The record gives no ordinance number or exact date. The official listing gives Ordinance No. 61 of 2025, dated 6 November 2025. This matches the Prothom Alo report that the notifications were issued 'on Thursday' (6 November 2025).
The record also leaves out the Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Ordinance, 2026 (Ordinance No. 23 of 2026). Digital Policy Alert dates it to 5 February 2026.
The Prothom Alo source's date field reads '2025-11'. The page metadata gives datePublished 2025-11-09.

laws.law: Privacy Act 1988 (No. 119, 1988)
laws.regulator: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC)
laws.note: Enacted as Act No. 119 of 1988 (commenced 1989) for Commonwealth agencies. The Privacy Amendment (Private Sector) Act 2000 extended it to private-sector organisations from 21 December 2001. It now covers most Australian Government agencies, organisations with annual turnover of more than AUD 3 million, and some smaller organisations.

sources.quote: The federal Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) ("Privacy Act") and the Australian Privacy Principles ("APPs") contained in the Privacy Act apply to private sector entities (including body corporates, partnerships, trusts and unincorporated associations) with an annual turnover of at least AUD $3 million, and all Commonwealth Government and Australian Capital Territory Government agencies.
sources.note: Law-firm global guide (secondary); used where the official gazette could not be read by script.

sources.institution: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC)
sources.title: The Privacy Act
sources.quote: The Privacy Act 1988 was introduced to promote and protect the privacy of individuals and to regulate how Australian Government agencies and organisations with an annual turnover of more than $3 million, and some other organisations, handle personal information.
sources.note: The regulator's own statement of coverage. Checked with fetch-text --check: FOUND.

sources.institution: Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC)
sources.title: History of the Privacy Act
sources.quote: In December 2000, the Privacy Amendment (Private Sector) Act 2000 extended coverage of the Privacy Act to some private sector organisations. The amendments commenced on 21 December 2001.
sources.note: The same page says: 'The Australian Parliament passed the Privacy Act 1988 at the end of 1988, and it commenced in 1989.' Checked with fetch-text --check: FOUND.

issues: The note says the Act applies to private-sector entities 'with annual turnover of at least AUD 3 million'. That wording comes from DLA Piper and is slightly wrong. Small business operators with turnover of $3 million or less are exempt, so coverage starts above $3 million. The OAIC says 'organisations with an annual turnover of more than $3 million, and some other organisations'. The note also leaves out the smaller organisations that are covered anyway, such as health service providers.

'The private sector was added by later amendment' is vague. The OAIC says the Privacy Amendment (Private Sector) Act 2000 extended coverage to some private-sector organisations from 21 December 2001. The OAIC also says the Act was passed at the end of 1988 and commenced in 1989.
The Act number (No. 119, 1988), the original coverage of Commonwealth agencies, and the OAIC as regulator all check out.

Also: 'the Privacy Act was enacted in 1993 to balance the desire of the state to make greater use of personal information held by government agencies, especially for data matching, with the need to protect the privacy of the individual in relation to that information.' The official legislation.govt.nz text is behind a script check (HTTP 202) and was not read.

issues: No errors found. The Law Commission Issues Paper 17 (March 2010) contains 'the Privacy Act 1993 came into force on 1 July 1993.' verbatim. It also quotes the long title, which covers 'The collection, use, and disclosure, by public and private sector agencies, of information relating to individuals'. That supports 'applying to agencies in both the public and private sectors'.

The DLA Piper quote is verbatim but only shows that the Privacy Act 2020 is now the governing law. The Privacy Commissioner's statement that the 2020 Act replaced the 1993 Act on 1 December 2020 is added as a direct source for 'replaced by the Privacy Act 2020'.

issues: No errors found. The PCPD 'Key Facts and History' page gives 'The Personal Data (Privacy) Ordinance (PDPO) was enacted on 3 August 1995' and, in its 1996 row, 'The PDPO came into force on 20 December 1996'. yearEnacted 1995, inForce 1996, the Cap. 486 title and the PCPD as regulator all match. The existing quote covers only the enactment date, so the in-force sentence from the same page is added as a second source.

'One of Asia's earliest comprehensive laws' has no source and is hedged. It is reasonable: Japan's 1988 act and Taiwan's 1995 act covered only computer-processed data or the public sector. A small caveat not worth a field change: s.33 of the PDPO, on cross-border transfers, has never been brought into force, so 'in force 20 December 1996' holds for the Ordinance generally, as the PCPD says.

laws.law: Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI, Act No. 57 of 2003)
laws.note: Promulgated in 2003 and fully in force in 2005, the APPI was Japan's first general data-protection law for the private sector. The public sector had its own legislation, first adopted in 1988 as the Act on the Protection of Computer-processed Personal Data Held by Administrative Organs. DLA Piper notes that the separate public-sector law was folded into the APPI with effect from 1 April 2022. Now supervised by the Personal Information Protection Commission.

sources.quote: the legislation for personal information protection in the public sector was first adopted as the “Act on the Protection of Computer-processed Personal Data Held by Administrative Organs”, which was promulgated in 1988.
sources.note: Primary (regulator's chairman). Supports the 1988 public-sector act. The speech goes on: 'Japan started drafting the Act on the Protection of Personal Information, which targeted the private sector' (also FOUND). --check FOUND.

sources.title: Privacy Culture and Data Protection Laws in Japan (speech by PPC Chairman Masao Horibe, ICDPPC 2017, Hong Kong)
sources.quote: the“Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI)” was promulgated in 2003 and enforced in 2005.
sources.note: Supports yearEnacted 2003 and inForce 2005. The missing space after 'the' is in the PDF text. --check FOUND.

sources.title: Data Protection Laws of the World — Japan
sources.quote: However, the data protection law for public sector was integrated into the APPI and became effective on April 1, 2022 (the data protection law for local governments became effective after April 1, 2023).
sources.note: Law-firm guide (secondary). Supports the 2022 merger of the public-sector law into the APPI. --check FOUND.

issues: Conflation: the note equates the DLA-cited 'separate data protection law for public sector' with the 1988 act. The DLA passage refers to the public-sector law that was merged into the APPI with effect from 1 April 2022, which was the 2003 Act on the Protection of Personal Information Held by Administrative Organs (Act No. 58 of 2003) that replaced the 1988 act. The 1988 act was the first public-sector law, not the one DLA describes.

'Japan's first law covering the private sector' is overstated. Earlier sectoral provisions existed, and the PPC's chairman describes the APPI as the general law drafted for the private sector. Changed to 'first general data-protection law for the private sector'.

The 1988 act (previously 'not verified here') is now sourced to a speech by PPC Chairman Masao Horibe on the PPC website. Added inForce 2005 (APPI 'promulgated in 2003 and enforced in 2005', same speech).

issues: The regulator is out of date. Since 1 February 2024 the supervisory authority has been the Direcção dos Serviços da Protecção de Dados Pessoais (DSPDP; English: Personal Data Protection Bureau, PDPB). It replaced the Gabinete para a Protecção de Dados Pessoais (GPDP), a temporary project team. The Macao government portal lists DSPDP as the department and 'PDPB' in its service names. DLA's authority page still says 'Office for Personal Data Protection (OPDP)', which is stale.

'Modelled on Portugal's law' was unsourced. Now sourced to C&C Advogados (Macau), which says Law 8/2005 was inspired by Portugal's 1998 law transposing Directive 95/46/EC. FPF's blog gives the Portuguese law as 'Law No. 68/98'; it is actually Lei 67/98, so FPF was not used.

issues: The core claims are correct: promulgated 29 March 2011, effective 30 September 2011 (koreanlii translation, FOUND).

The predecessor public-agency act (1994), previously marked 'not verified here', is now verified. PIPA's Addenda Article 2 repeals the 'Act on the Protection of Personal Information Maintained by Public Agencies', and a 2024 peer-reviewed article dates that act to 1994.

'Substantially amended again in March 2026' had no source. It is correct only as the promulgation date: the National Assembly passed the amendment on 12 February 2026, it was promulgated on 10 March 2026, and most provisions take effect on 11 September 2026. frameworks.name: Guidelines on the Protection of Privacy and Transborder Flows of Personal Data
frameworks.parties: Adopted by the OECD Council on 23 September 1980 as a Recommendation to member countries (not legally binding), which also invites non-members to adhere; revised on 11 July 2013. The number of adherents was not verified here.
frameworks.note: The OECD calls them 'the first internationally agreed-upon set of privacy principles', although the Council of Europe had adopted resolutions on data-bank privacy principles in 1973 and 1974. There are eight principles: collection limitation, data quality, purpose specification, use limitation, security safeguards, openness, individual participation and accountability. APEC's first Privacy Framework was 'modelled upon' them, as was Hong Kong's 1995 ordinance, which followed a law-reform recommendation for a law 'based on the OECD Privacy Guidelines 1980'. The OECD says they have influenced legislation 'in OECD countries and beyond'.

frameworks.name: Convention for the Protection of Individuals with regard to Automatic Processing of Personal Data (ETS No. 108)
frameworks.parties: Opened for signature at Strasbourg on 28 January 1981; in force 1 October 1985. States outside the Council of Europe may accede when invited by its Committee of Ministers. In November 2020 the Council of Europe counted 55 countries bound: all 47 of its member states plus eight non-European states (Argentina, Cabo Verde, Mauritius, Mexico, Morocco, Senegal, Tunisia, Uruguay), with Burkina Faso's accession pending. The current total was not verified.
frameworks.note: Still the only binding international data-protection treaty open to any country (in a 2020 Council of Europe presentation's words, 'no other binding instrument in the field open to any country'). Uruguay, whose accession took effect on 1 August 2013, was the first non-European party.

That copy prints 'this convention' in lower case; the check is case-insensitive.

Party count made precise. The record gave only the eight non-European parties 'around 2019'. The same INAI document also says all 47 Council of Europe member states were parties ('los 47 Estados miembros del Consejo de Europa son Parte del Convenio 108'). A Council of Europe data-protection presentation of 10 November 2020, hosted by the WTO, gives '55 countries bound by the Convention' (the same eight non-European states plus 47 CoE members), with Burkina Faso pending. Both quotes FOUND. The current (2026) total is still not verified.

The note's two claims had no source on the record; both are now sourced. 'Only binding ... treaty open to any country': the 2020 CoE presentation says 'UNIQUE (no other binding instrument in the field open to any country)'. 'Uruguay (2013) first non-European accession': PL&B reports the CoE announcement that Uruguay's accession entered into force on 1 August 2013, 'making it the 45th state to become a party, and the first non-European party'. Both quotes FOUND. Non-member accession is by invitation of the Committee of Ministers (Article 23, FOUND in the Irish copy), so 'open to any country' means open to invitation.

Added the entry into force (1 October 1985), confirmed in the UN Treaty Series registration (FOUND). Opening for signature on 28 January 1981 is correct (UNTS: 'Concluded at Strasbourg on 28 January 1981', FOUND). The INAI quote was re-fetched and FOUND.

frameworks.name: Guidelines for the Regulation of Computerized Personal Data Files (UNGA resolution 45/95)

frameworks.note: Ten minimum principles, applying 'to all public and private computerized files', including the designation of a supervisory authority. In July 2024 the UN Special Rapporteur on the right to privacy, Ana Brian Nougrères, proposed updating them (report A/79/173).

sources.note: --check FOUND on 2026-09-23 (the PDF uses curly quotes; the tool normalises them). Distributed 17 July 2024 for the 79th session and submitted under HRC resolution 28/16. Supports the 2024 update claim and gives a UN primary for the 14 December 1990 date.

issues: Both EPIC quotes re-fetched and FOUND. The EPIC page also supports the note's quoted phrase 'to all public and private computerized files' and the supervisory-authority principle ('responsible for supervising observance of the principles set forth above'). Resolution 45/95 and the date 14 December 1990 are correct.

Unsourced claim: 'In 2024 the UN Special Rapporteur on privacy proposed updating them' had no source. It is true. Report A/79/173 of 17 July 2024 by Special Rapporteur Ana Brian Nougrères 'sets out a proposal for the updating of General Assembly resolution 45/95 of 14 December 1990' (FOUND on the UN ODS PDF). The source is added, and it also gives a UN primary for the adoption date.

Minor: the Guidelines apply 'in the first place' to computerized files, extend optionally to manual files, and have a separate Part B for files kept by international organizations. The note's quote is accurate but partial. No change is needed.

frameworks.name: Directive 95/46/EC on the protection of individuals with regard to the processing of personal data
frameworks.parties: Binding on all EU (and, via the EEA, EEA) member states; adopted 24 October 1995; repealed by the GDPR from 25 May 2018.
frameworks.note: A directive (binding as to result, transposed by national laws). Its Article 25 allowed personal data to go to a third country only if that country 'ensures an adequate level of protection', with exceptions in Article 26. The Commission later found Argentina (2003), Israel (2011), Uruguay (2012) and New Zealand (2012) adequate, which gave trading partners a commercial reason to adopt or update EU-style laws. Israel's core statute (1981) and New Zealand's Privacy Act predate the Directive, although New Zealand amended its Act in 2010. Covered in detail in the internet slice.

The Commission's own adequacy decisions show that at least two of those laws predate the Directive. The adequacy findings themselves are confirmed: Argentina (2003/490/EC), Israel (2011/61/EU of 31 January 2011), Uruguay (2012/484/EU of 21 August 2012) and New Zealand (2013/65/EU of 19 December 2012). The note is rewritten to state these findings and to drop the blanket causal claim.

'Barred transfers ... without adequate protection' left out Article 26, which lets transfers to non-adequate countries take place under listed conditions ('By way of derogation from Article 25', FOUND). The note now says so.

Both sources are Wayback copies of EUR-Lex that could not be re-fetched (web.archive.org reset every connection; live EUR-Lex returns a bot challenge), so both are set to PENDING. Both quotes are FOUND on legislation.gov.uk copies of the same texts, which are added: the Article 7(a) quote in the consolidated Directive, and the Argentina Article 1 quote in the adopted Decision.

Checked and correct: adoption on 24 October 1995 ('of 24 October 1995', FOUND); repeal with effect from 25 May 2018 (GDPR Article 94, FOUND). The bindingness value 'regulation' is the slice's category for binding EU law; the note already explains that this is a directive. No change is needed there.

frameworks.name: APEC Privacy Framework
frameworks.parties: Endorsed by APEC ministers (all member economies) in November 2004; published 2005; updated 2015.
frameworks.note: Nine principles derived from the OECD Guidelines, including a distinctive 'preventing harm' principle and an accountability principle. It creates no obligation to legislate.

sources.title: APEC Privacy Framework
sources.quote: The APEC Privacy Framework promotes a flexible approach to information privacy protection across APEC member economies, while avoiding the creation of unnecessary barriers to information flows.

sources.institution: Office of the Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data, Hong Kong (Tony Lam, Acting Privacy Commissioner)

sources.quote: APEC Leaders endorsed the Ministerial Joint Statement in full at the 12th APEC Economic Leaders' meeting held in November 2004 at Santiago, Chile.
sources.note: --check FOUND on 2026-09-23. The preceding sentence reads: 'The 2004 APEC Ministerial Joint Statement endorsed the APEC Privacy Framework and the Future Work Agenda on Implementation of the APEC Privacy Framework.' (FOUND).

sources.title: APEC Privacy Framework (2015)
sources.quote: The previous version of the Framework (2005) was modelled upon the OECD Guidelines (1980) which at that time represented the international consensus on what constitutes fair and trustworthy treatment of personal information. The updated Framework (2015) draws upon concepts introduced into the OECD Guidelines (2013)
sources.note: Para. 5. --check FOUND. Supports both 'derived from the OECD Guidelines' and 'updated 2015'. The PDF is © 2017 APEC Secretariat and was published in August 2017.

sources.title: APEC Privacy Framework
sources.quote: In practice, the Framework is meant to be implemented in a flexible manner that can accommodate various methods of implementation, including through central authorities, multi-agency enforcement bodies, a network of designated industry bodies, or a combination of the above, as Member Economies deem appropriate.
sources.note: Part IV, para. 31. --check FOUND. The paragraph opens: 'There are several options for giving effect to the Framework and securing privacy protections for individuals including legislative, administrative, industry' (FOUND; the next word, 'self-regulatory', is split across a line in the PDF). Supports 'creates no obligation to legislate'.

issues: No factual error found, but the record's one source (the 2005 Framework PDF, quote FOUND) supports none of the dated claims. That PDF says only 'Ministers have endorsed', with no date, and does not mention the 2015 update. Sources are added for the November 2004 endorsement, the 2015 update, the OECD lineage and the 'no obligation to legislate' point.

November 2004: the Hong Kong PCPD's 2005 overview says the 2004 APEC Ministerial Joint Statement endorsed the Framework and that Leaders endorsed that statement in November 2004 in Santiago (FOUND). APEC's news release is dated 'Santiago, Chile | 20 November 2004', but the tool cannot extract its body. The ministerial meeting itself was on 17–18 November 2004 (2004/AMM/014rev1, used on the event record).

Checked and correct: nine principles (headings I–IX in the 2005 PDF: Preventing Harm, Notice, Collection Limitation, Uses of Personal Information, Choice, Integrity of Personal Information, Security Safeguards, Access and Correction, Accountability). Published December 2005 (APEC publication page). Updated 2015: the updated Framework calls itself 'The updated Framework (2015)' and says the previous version 'was modelled upon the OECD Guidelines (1980)'. No obligation to legislate: para. 31 lists legislative, administrative, industry self-regulatory or combined options.

frameworks.name: APEC Cross-Border Privacy Rules (CBPR) System
frameworks.parties: Nine participating economies (as stated on the CBPR site): the United States, Mexico, Japan, Canada, Singapore, the Republic of Korea, Australia, Chinese Taipei and the Philippines.
frameworks.note: Companies are certified against the APEC principles by approved third-party 'Accountability Agents' and enforced by participating authorities under the Cross-border Privacy Enforcement Arrangement (CPEA).

sources.title: About CBPRs
sources.quote: The APEC Cross-Border Privacy Rules (CBPR) System, endorsed by APEC Leaders in 2011, is a voluntary, accountability-based system that facilitates privacy-respecting data flows among APEC economies.

sources.title: About CBPRs
sources.quote: There are currently nine participating APEC CBPR system economies: USA, Mexico, Japan, Canada, Singapore, the Republic of Korea, Australia, Chinese Taipei, and the Philippines
sources.note: The page's list of the nine economies continues after the colon; not all names were checked verbatim.

issues: No factual error. Both quotes re-fetched and FOUND. The page lists the nine economies in the record's order: 'USA, Mexico, Japan, Canada, Singapore, the Republic of Korea, Australia, Chinese Taipei, and the Philippines'. The source note said not all names were checked verbatim, so source 1's quote is extended to include the full list (FOUND).

Checked and correct: Leaders' endorsement in 2011; Accountability Agents certify companies; enforcement runs through the CPEA ('A regulatory cooperative arrangement (the CPEA) to ensure that each of the APEC CBPR system program requirements can be enforced by participating APEC economies', on the same page). The FTC dates Leaders' endorsement to 13 November 2011 in Honolulu (event record). The Global CBPR Forum (2022) has its own framework record, so its absence here is not an error.

frameworks.name: International Standards on the Protection of Personal Data and Privacy (Madrid Resolution)
frameworks.body: International Conference of Data Protection and Privacy Commissioners (now Global Privacy Assembly)
frameworks.parties: Welcomed by the Conference on 5 November 2009; drafted by authorities from fifty countries.
frameworks.note: A regulators' draft for a future binding global instrument, which never followed.

sources.institution: International Conference of Data Protection and Privacy Commissioners (hosted by the Global Privacy Assembly)
sources.title: The Madrid Resolution
sources.quote: The joint efforts of the privacy guarantors from fifty countries, coordinated by the Spanish Data Protection Agency, has resulted in a text that seeks to reflect the many approaches that the protection of this right allows for, by integrating legislations on five continents.

sources.note: Presentation page. --check FOUND on 2026-09-23. Supports the parties field's date and 'welcomed'.

sources.institution: International Conference of Data Protection and Privacy Commissioners (hosted by the Global Privacy Assembly)
sources.title: The Madrid Resolution
sources.quote: The Joint Proposal demonstrates the feasibility of such standards, as a new step towards the development of a binding international instrument in due course.
sources.note: Operative paragraph of the resolution. --check FOUND. Supports the note's 'draft for a future binding global instrument'.

issues: The one source quote supports only 'fifty countries'. The parties field's date and verb ('Welcomed by the Conference on 5 November 2009') and the note's 'draft for a future binding global instrument' were unsupported on the record, although the same PDF states both. Those two quotes are added (both FOUND).

Checked and correct: the name matches the cover ('International Standards on the Protection of Personal Data and Privacy — The Madrid Resolution'). The body was renamed the Global Privacy Assembly in 2019 (see the event record for the first conference). 'Drafted by authorities from fifty countries' matches 'the privacy guarantors from fifty countries, coordinated by the Spanish Data Protection Agency'. 'Which never followed' is a judgement about the absence of a later instrument; no binding global instrument built on the Madrid text is known.

frameworks.name: Supplementary Act A/SA.1/01/10 on Personal Data Protection within ECOWAS
frameworks.body: Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS)
frameworks.parties: Adopted at the 37th session of the ECOWAS Authority of Heads of State and Government and signed at Abuja on 16 February 2010. The signature page carries 13 signatures, several by ministers on behalf of their presidents; Guinea and Niger are not among them. Annexed to the ECOWAS Treaty as an integral part of it, the Act binds all member states (15 in 2010).
frameworks.note: Article 2 requires each member state to establish 'a legal framework of protection for privacy of data'. Article 14 requires each to set up its own data-protection authority, 'an independent administrative authority'. It came four years before the African Union's continental Malabo Convention (2014).

sources.quote: HAVE SIGNED THIS SUPPLEMENTARY ACT DONE AT ABUJA ON 16TH DAYOF FEBRUARY 2010 IN A SINGLE ORIGINAL IN ENGLISH, FRENCH AND PORTUGUESE
sources.note: Scanned copy with OCR errors ('DAYOF', 'A1SA.1f01f10' for A/SA.1/01/10); quote reproduces the OCR text layer.

Article 2: 'Each Member State shall establish a legal framework of protection for' (FOUND; the OCR renders the next word as 'prrvacy').

sources.note: --check FOUND. The signature block that follows is OCR'd with errors. It shows 13 signatories: Benin, Burkina Faso, Cabo Verde, Côte d'Ivoire, the Gambia, Ghana, Guinea-Bissau, Mali, Liberia, Nigeria, Senegal, Sierra Leone and Togo. Article 48: 'This Supplementary Act shall be annexed to the ECOWAS Treaty of which it shall be an integral part' (OCR 'lI1e' for 'the', so it is not checked verbatim).

issues: Unsupported 'first'. No source is given for 'The first sub-regional harmonisation instrument in Africa', and the claim depends on what counts as a harmonisation instrument. It is removed. What the sources do support is that the Act came before the AU's Malabo Convention (2014), whose date is sourced on framework au-malabo-convention-2014.

Unsupported and doubtful: 'the model for many francophone West African laws'. No source is given, and the slice's own law records show several francophone West African laws that predate the Act: Burkina Faso 2004 (bf-2004), Senegal 2008 (sn-2008) and Benin 2009 (bj-2009). The claim is removed.

Imprecise: 'Signed by the Heads of State and Government'. The testimonium does read 'WE, THE HEADS OF STATE AND GOVERNMENT ... HAVE SIGNED' (FOUND). But the OCR'd signature page shows 13 signatures, several made by ministers or a vice-president on behalf of heads of state: Benin, Burkina Faso, Cabo Verde, Côte d'Ivoire, the Gambia, Ghana, Guinea-Bissau, Mali, Liberia, Nigeria, Senegal, Sierra Leone and Togo. Guinea and Niger are absent. The Act is annexed to the ECOWAS Treaty 'of which it shall be an integral part', so it binds all member states. The parties field is made precise.

Checked and correct: document number A/SA.1/01/10 (OCR 'A1SA.1f01f10'); Abuja, 16 February 2010, at the 37th session of the Authority (header FOUND). Article 2 requires each member state to 'establish a legal framework of protection for' data privacy. Article 14 requires each to establish its own data protection authority (FOUND), which is 'an independent administrative authority' (FOUND). ECOWAS had 15 members in 2010.

frameworks.name: SADC Model Law on Data Protection
frameworks.body: Southern African Development Community (with ITU/EU HIPSSA project)
frameworks.parties: Adopted by SADC ministers responsible for telecommunications, postal and ICT in Mauritius in November 2012.
frameworks.note: A model text for national legislators, not a treaty. Usually cited as 2013, the year the ITU published the final text; an ITU draft is dated March 2011. The text itself records validation at a workshop in Gaborone (27 February–3 March 2012) and adoption by SADC ICT ministers in Mauritius in November 2012.

sources.title: Data Protection: Southern African Development Community (SADC) Model Law
sources.quote: It was further adopted by the SADC Ministers responsible for Telecommunications, Postal and ICT at their meeting in Mauritius in November 2012.

sources.title: DRAFT Southern African Development Community (SADC) Model Law on Data Protection (March 2011)
sources.quote: DRAFT Southern African Development Community (SADC) MODEL LAW ON DATA PROTECTION March 2011
sources.note: The draft's cover page, which shows a March 2011 draft before the 2012 validation and adoption. --check FOUND.

sources.title: Introductory Modules on Digital Rights and Freedom of Expression Online — Module 4: Data Protection
sources.quote: HIPSSA, ‘Data Protection: SADC Model Law’ (2013)
sources.note: Secondary source. Shows the usual citation year (2013), not 2010. The page also heads the entry 'SADC Data Protection Model Law 2013'. --check FOUND.

issues: Source quote re-checked FOUND verbatim in the ITU/HIPSSA final text (Geneva, 2013). The year, the Gaborone validation (27 February to 3 March 2012) and the Mauritius ministerial adoption (November 2012) are all correct.

The note's claim that the text is 'often dated 2010, when drafting began' is unsupported. The ITU final text never mentions 2010. ITU's own draft is dated March 2011, and secondary literature (e.g. Media Defence) usually cites the model law as 2013, the year ITU published it. Note rewritten to say only what the sources support.

frameworks.name: African Union Convention on Cyber Security and Personal Data Protection (Malabo Convention)
frameworks.parties: Adopted 27 June 2014 by the 23rd AU Assembly in Malabo; in force 8 June 2023, after Mauritania deposited the 15th ratification on 9 May 2023. The 15 parties at entry into force were Angola, Cape Verde, Côte d'Ivoire, Congo, Ghana, Guinea, Mauritania, Mauritius, Mozambique, Namibia, Niger, Rwanda, Senegal, Togo and Zambia; São Tomé and Príncipe made 16 in February 2024. Benin has signed but not ratified.
frameworks.note: Combines personal-data protection with e-commerce and cyber-security/cyber-crime rules. It is Africa's continent-wide data-protection treaty, but not the region's first binding instrument: the ECOWAS Supplementary Act on Personal Data Protection (2010) already bound West African states.

sources.institution: Centre for Intellectual Property and Information Technology Law (CIPIT), Strathmore University
sources.title: The African Union Convention on Cyber Security and Personal Data Protection: Key Insights
sources.quote: The Malabo Convention entered into force on 8 June 2023 after receiving the required minimum of 15 ratifications from AU Member States

sources.quote: Adopted by the Twentythird Ordinary Session of the Assembly, held in Malabo, Equatorial Guinea, 27th June 2014.
sources.note: The PDF's table columns are scrambled in the extracted text, so the post-2023 ratification count could not be read reliably.

sources.title: Africa: AU’s Malabo Convention set to enter force after nine years
sources.quote: The AU’s latest status list on the Malabo Convention, dated 12 May 2023, lists the following 15 states as having submitted ratification: Angola (11 May 2020), Cape Verde (5 February 2022), Côte d’Ivoire (3 April 2023), Congo (23 October 2020), Ghana (3 June 2019), Guinea (16 October 2018), Mozambique (21 January 2020), Mauritania (9 May 2023), Mauritius (14 March 2018), Namibia (1 February 2019), Niger (16 March 2022), Rwanda (21 November 2019), Senegal (16 August 2016), Togo (19 October 2021), and Zambia (24 March 2021).
sources.note: --check FOUND. The same page lists Benin among states that 'signed the Malabo Convention without yet ratifying it' (FOUND), and says the Convention covers 'electronic commerce, data protection, and cybercrime and cybersecurity' (FOUND).

sources.title: Introductory Modules on Digital Rights and Freedom of Expression Online — Module 4: Data Protection
sources.quote: This instrument is designed to be directly transposed into a domestic context among West African states and provides in detail the conditions for the lawful processing of personal information and the rights of data subjects. Importantly, it is also legally binding on ECOWAS States.
sources.note: About the ECOWAS Supplementary Act on Personal Data Protection (2010). Refutes the claim that Malabo is the only binding regional data-protection instrument outside Europe. --check FOUND.

issues: Wrong party list: the 'parties' field names Benin as one of the 15 ratifying states, copying an error in the CIPIT blog. The AU's own status list (08/07/2024) shows Benin only as a signatory (signed 28/01/2015, no ratification), and shows Angola ratified (21/02/2020, deposited 11/05/2020). The 15 parties at entry into force were Angola, Cape Verde, Côte d'Ivoire, Congo, Ghana, Guinea, Mauritania, Mauritius, Mozambique, Namibia, Niger, Rwanda, Senegal, Togo and Zambia. Two sources agree: ALT Advisory's Data Protection Africa, which uses the AU status list of 12 May 2023, and my own coordinate-based reconstruction of the AU PDF table.

The AU status list of 8 July 2024 gives 'of ratification : 16': São Tomé and Príncipe ratified 25/09/2023 and deposited 15/02/2024. The earlier note said this count 'could not be read'. It can be read from the PDF text.

Overstated 'only': the note calls Malabo 'the only binding regional data-protection treaty outside Europe'. The ECOWAS Supplementary Act A/SA.1/01/10 on Personal Data Protection (2010) is a binding regional instrument on West African states. Media Defence: 'Importantly, it is also legally binding on ECOWAS States.' Note reworded.

The adoption date of 27 June 2014 is confirmed by the note on the AU status list and by the AU treaty page ('Date of Adoption Fri, 27 Jun 2014'). The entry into force on 8 June 2023 is confirmed: Mauritania deposited the 15th instrument on 9 May 2023.

frameworks.name: General Data Protection Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR)
frameworks.parties: Adopted in 2016; directly applicable in all EU member states from 25 May 2018, and extended to the EEA EFTA states (Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway) in July 2018.
frameworks.note: Replaced the 1995 Directive; its extraterritorial reach and fines made it a reference model for Brazil, Kenya, Nigeria, Thailand and others. Covered in other slices.

sources.title: Data Protection Laws of the World — Sweden (EU regulation section)
sources.quote: The General Data Protection Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2016/679) ( GDPR ) is a European Union law which entered into force in 2016 and, following a two year transition period, became directly applicable law in all Member States of the European Union on 25 May 2018, without requiring implementation by the EU Member States through national law.
sources.note: Law-firm global guide (secondary).

sources.note: Supports the EEA extension in July 2018, not 25 May 2018. EFTA's own news item (entry into force in the EEA EFTA states on 20 July 2018) returned HTTP 403. --check FOUND.

issues: Source quote re-checked FOUND on the DLA Piper Sweden page. Year 2016 and application from 25 May 2018 are correct (GDPR Art. 99).

'(and in the EEA)' implies the GDPR applied in the EEA from 25 May 2018. It did not. It was incorporated into the EEA Agreement by the EEA Joint Committee on 6 July 2018 and entered into force in Iceland, Liechtenstein and Norway in mid-July 2018 (20 July per EFTA; efta.int returns 403 to scripts, so the secondary 'mid-July' wording is used).

The note's unsourced list of countries for which the GDPR was 'the reference model' includes India. India's Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023 departs substantially from the GDPR (e.g. consent plus 'legitimate uses' instead of six lawful bases, and no special-category regime), so presenting the GDPR as India's model overstates the case. India removed; 'the' softened to 'a'.

frameworks.note: A model for Latin American and Iberian legislators, drafted with the EU's GDPR as an explicit reference point. The 2026 update, approved at the RIPD meeting in Cartagena de Indias (Colombia), is to be sent to SEGIB for possible adoption at the Ibero-American Summit of Heads of State and Government in Madrid (4–5 November 2026).

frameworks.name: Protocol amending Convention 108 (CETS No. 223) — 'Convention 108+'
frameworks.parties: Opened for signature in Strasbourg in October 2018; 25 ratifications by 15 June 2023 (Slovakia the 25th). Moldova deposited its ratification on 15 May 2026, which the Council of Europe reported as the 34th; the Protocol needs 38 Parties to enter into force.
frameworks.note: Modernises Convention 108 for the GDPR era. Mauritius was the first non-European state to ratify it (4 September 2020, the sixth ratification overall and the first in Africa); Uruguay's parliament approved it in 2021. Not in force as a whole as of the latest verified data.

frameworks.name: Global Cross-Border Privacy Rules (CBPR) Forum

policyModels.name: Omnibus, rights-based data protection (the European model)
policyModels.description: One general law covers public and private sectors alike; data protection is treated as a fundamental right; processing needs a legal basis; an independent authority supervises; and transfers abroad are restricted unless the destination is 'adequate' or other safeguards (such as standard contractual clauses) are in place. It began with Hesse (1970), Sweden (1973) and Convention 108 (1981), was harmonised by the 1995 Directive and the GDPR (2016), and was exported through adequacy decisions and treaty accession. Consent here is one lawful basis among several, not the whole system.

sources.institution: European Parliament (text as published in the Official Journal of the European Communities, C 364/1)
sources.title: Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union (2000/C 364/01) — Article 8: Protection of personal data
sources.quote: 1. Everyone has the right to the protection of personal data concerning him or her. 2. Such data must be processed fairly for specified purposes and on the basis of the consent of the person concerned or some other legitimate basis laid down by law.
sources.note: The FRA URL (https://fra.europa.eu/en/eu-charter/article/8-protection-personal-data) now returns a bot-verification page, so it cannot be checked by script. The same quote is --check FOUND verbatim in this OJ text of the Charter. Article 8 is unchanged in the 2012 consolidated version.

sources.title: Anu Bradford, Digital Empires: The Global Battle to Regulate Technology (Oxford University Press, 2023) — book page
sources.quote: Bradford examines three competing regulatory approaches — the American market-driven model, the Chinese state-driven model, and the European rights-driven regulatory model — and discusses how governments and tech companies navigate the inevitable conflicts that arise when these regulatory approaches collide in the international domain.

sources.institution: gdpr-info.eu (Intersoft Consulting; reproduces the official text of Regulation (EU) 2016/679)
sources.title: Art. 46 GDPR — Transfers subject to appropriate safeguards
sources.quote: In the absence of a decision pursuant to Article 45 (3), a controller or processor may transfer personal data to a third country or an international organisation only if the controller or processor has provided appropriate safeguards
sources.note: Shows that adequacy is not the only transfer route (SCCs, BCRs, codes, certification). EUR-Lex serves a JS challenge to scripts. --check FOUND.

issues: Source 0 (FRA Charter page) could not be re-verified. fra.europa.eu now serves a 'Verification Required' bot-challenge page, so --check returns NOT-FOUND. The identical Article 8 text is FOUND verbatim in the Charter as published in the Official Journal (C 364, 18.12.2000) on europarl.europa.eu, so the source has been moved there. Article 8 wording is unchanged in the 2012 consolidated Charter.

Oversimplification: 'transfers abroad are restricted unless the destination is adequate' omits the GDPR's other transfer routes. Art. 46 allows transfers without adequacy where appropriate safeguards (SCCs, BCRs, etc.) are in place. Description amended and sourced.
The Bradford book-page quote re-checked FOUND. The page confirms Oxford University Press, publication date 9-2023.
Minor, not changed: Hesse's 1970 act covered only the Land's public administration, so it is an ancestor of the omnibus model rather than an example of one. 'It began with' is acceptable as lineage.

policyModels.name: Sectoral laws plus notice-and-choice (the American model)
policyModels.description: No general federal law for the private sector. Federal statutes cover particular sectors or harms (credit reports, health records, children online, video rentals), the Privacy Act 1974 covers federal agencies, and the FTC polices unfair or deceptive practices, so a company's own privacy notice becomes the enforceable promise. Since California's 2018 CCPA, states have added comprehensive consumer laws built largely on opt-out rights. Scholars call the underlying logic 'privacy self-management': individuals are expected to read notices and choose.
exemplars: US states with comprehensive consumer privacy laws since 2018 (California first)

sources.title: Data Protection Laws of the World — United States
sources.quote: There is no comprehensive national privacy law in the United States. However, the US does have a number of largely sector-specific privacy and data security laws at the federal level, as well as many more at the state (and local) level.

sources.title: Introduction: Privacy Self-Management and the Consent Dilemma, 126 Harv. L. Rev. 1880
sources.quote: I will refer to this approach to privacy regulation as “privacy self-management.” Privacy self-management takes refuge in consent.

sources.title: Anu Bradford, Digital Empires: The Global Battle to Regulate Technology (Oxford University Press, 2023) — book page
sources.quote: Bradford examines three competing regulatory approaches — the American market-driven model, the Chinese state-driven model, and the European rights-driven regulatory model — and discusses how governments and tech companies navigate the inevitable conflicts that arise when these regulatory approaches collide in the international domain.

sources.title: Data Protection Laws of the World — United States
sources.quote: In recent years, beginning with California in 2018, states have begun to introduce and enact their own comprehensive privacy laws.
sources.note: --check FOUND. Supports 'Since California's 2018 CCPA, states have added comprehensive consumer laws'.

sources.title: Data Protection Laws of the World — United States
sources.quote: Making materially inaccurate or misleading privacy and security statements, including in privacy policies
sources.note: --check FOUND. A bullet in the list of FTC unfair/deceptive-practice enforcement grounds. Supports 'a company's own privacy notice becomes the enforceable promise'.

issues: No factual error found. Checked each claim. There is no comprehensive federal law. The sectoral statutes (credit reporting, healthcare, children's online privacy, VPPA video rentals) are named on the DLA Piper page. The FTC's unfair-or-deceptive authority reaches 'misleading privacy and security statements, including in privacy policies'. The state wave began 'with California in 2018' (DLA Piper). 'Privacy self-management' is Solove's term (126 Harv. L. Rev. 1880, May 2013). The Privacy Act 1974 covering federal agencies is standard and uncontested.
The description's CCPA/2018 and FTC-privacy-notice claims were not directly carried by any quoted source; supporting quotes from the same DLA Piper page are added below.
Minor: the Bradford book page gives Publication Date 9-2023; date refined.

policyModels.name: Accountability and certification (the APEC model)
policyModels.description: Principles-based and voluntary between states: the APEC Privacy Framework (2004) asks each economy to implement nine principles as it sees fit, with a strong emphasis on not obstructing information flows. The organisation is held 'accountable' for its own practices, including after transfer, and can be certified by an Accountability Agent (a public or private body recognised by the participating economies) under the Cross-Border Privacy Rules (2011); the Global CBPR Forum (2022) aims to take this beyond APEC. It trades uniform individual rights for interoperability between very different national laws.
exemplars: APEC CBPR economies: United States, Japan, Singapore, Korea, Canada, Mexico, Australia, Chinese Taipei, Philippines
Global CBPR Forum members and associates

sources.title: APEC Privacy Framework — Principle IX, Accountability
sources.quote: A personal information controller should be accountable for complying with measures that give effect to the Principles stated above.

sources.title: About CBPRs
sources.quote: The APEC Cross-Border Privacy Rules (CBPR) System, endorsed by APEC Leaders in 2011, is a voluntary, accountability-based system that facilitates privacy-respecting data flows among APEC economies.

sources.note: --check FOUND. The header reads '16th APEC Ministerial Meeting Santiago, Chile 17-18 November 2004' (also FOUND). APEC's press release 'APEC Ministers Endorse the APEC Privacy Framework' (apec.org/Press/News-Releases/2004/1120_apecminsendorseprivacyfrmwk) is datelined 20 November 2004 in its raw HTML. sources.note: --check FOUND. Supports 'implement nine principles as it sees fit'.

sources.quote: The Global CBPR Forum was established in 2022, by Australia, Canada, Japan, the Republic of Korea, Mexico, the Philippines, Singapore, Chinese Taipei, and the United States of America, as jurisdictions participating in the APEC CBPR System at the time, to support the free flow of data and effective data protection and privacy globally.

issues: 'certified by a private Accountability Agent' is wrong. The official CBPR site says Accountability Agents may be 'public or private', and several are public bodies (Korea's is the Korea Internet & Security Agency, a government agency, listed on cbprs.org/business).

The 2004 date, the Global CBPR Forum (2022), the 'as it sees fit' flexibility and the after-transfer accountability were not carried by any quoted source. Sources are added: APEC's 2004 Ministerial document (Santiago, 17-18 Nov 2004), the Global CBPR Forum 'About' page, and APEC Framework paras 31 and 26 (commentary).
Otherwise verified: nine principles (Preventing Harm to Accountability, I-IX, in the PDF), CBPR endorsed by APEC Leaders in 2011, and the nine CBPR economies exactly as listed (cbprs.org).

policyModels.name: State-security and data-sovereignty model
policyModels.description: Strong rules bind companies, often with GDPR-like individual rights, but the state keeps broad access for security purposes, and personal data is treated as a national resource: Russia requires its citizens' data to be recorded and stored in databases inside the country, and China requires critical operators and large-volume processors to store data at home and pass a state security assessment before exporting it. Russia's 2014 localisation law and China's Cybersecurity Law (2016) and PIPL (2021) are the defining cases; Bradford calls China's version 'state-driven'. Several other countries have since copied localisation or security-assessment rules.

sources.institution: ProMarket (Stigler Center, University of Chicago) — excerpt from Anu Bradford, Digital Empires
sources.title: Digital Empires (book excerpt)
sources.quote: In contrast to the American market-driven regulatory model, the Chinese regulatory model rests on a state-driven vision for the digital economy.

sources.institution: National People's Congress of the PRC
sources.title: 中华人民共和国个人信息保护法 — Article 40
sources.quote: 第四十条 关键信息基础设施运营者和处理个人信息达到国家网信部门规定数量的个人信息处理者，应当将在中华人民共和国境内收集和产生的个人信息存储在境内。确需向境外提供的，应当通过国家网信部门组织的安全评估
sources.note: Translation: 'Article 40: Critical information infrastructure operators and personal information processors that process personal information in quantities reaching thresholds set by the national cyberspace department shall store domestically personal information collected and produced within the PRC.'

sources.title: Федеральный закон от 21.07.2014 г. № 242-ФЗ
sources.quote: При сборе персональных данных, в том числе посредством информационно-телекоммуникационной сети "Интернет", оператор обязан обеспечить запись, систематизацию, накопление, хранение, уточнение (обновление, изменение), извлечение персональных данных граждан Российской Федерации с использованием баз данных, находящихся на территории Российской Федерации
sources.note: Translation: '...retrieval of personal data of citizens of the Russian Federation using databases located in the territory of the Russian Federation'.

sources.institution: ProMarket (Stigler Center, University of Chicago) — excerpt from Anu Bradford, Digital Empires
sources.title: Digital Empires (book excerpt)
sources.quote: Chinese tech companies have acted as the CCP’s surrogates, performing the surveillance and control functions of the state over their users.
sources.note: --check FOUND. Supports 'the state keeps broad access for security purposes' for the Chinese case.

issues: Overgeneralised: 'personal data is treated as a national resource that must be stored at home or exported only after state security review'. PIPL Art. 40 applies the store-at-home and security-assessment rule only to critical information infrastructure operators and processors above CAC volume thresholds. Other processors may export under Art. 38 by standard contract or certification. Russia's 242-FZ requires citizens' data to be recorded and stored in databases in Russia, but it does not impose a state security review on export.
The PIPL quote was cut off before the sentence that actually carries the 'security review' claim. It is extended with '确需向境外提供的，应当通过国家网信部门组织的安全评估' (--check FOUND).
'The state keeps broad access for security purposes' had no support. A Bradford excerpt quote from the same ProMarket page is added.

Verified: 242-FZ is dated 21.07.2014 and came into force 1 September 2015 (kremlin.ru). It amends 152-FZ of 27 July 2006, which confirms the '152-FZ 2006' exemplar. PIPL was adopted 20 Aug 2021 and in force 1 Nov 2021 (Art. 74). ProMarket excerpt date 2024-04-11 (article:published_time).

policyModels.name: Constitutional habeas data (the Latin American route)
policyModels.description: The individual gets a constitutional writ, modelled on habeas corpus, to go to court, see what a databank holds about them, and demand correction or deletion. It is a remedy the person sets in motion rather than a regulator's licensing system. Brazil created it in 1988; Paraguay (1992), Peru (1993) and Argentina (1994) followed, then Ecuador and Colombia. General data-protection statutes and regulators came later: Argentina's law in 2000 (its regulator set up under a 2001 decree) and Brazil's LGPD in 2018.

sources.institution: Journal of Information, Law & Technology (JILT), University of Warwick — Andrés Guadamuz
sources.title: Habeas Data: The Latin-American Response to Data Protection (JILT 2000(2))
sources.quote: Some Latin-American countries have enacted a new type of constitutional protection of personal data in order to insure individual privacy from the abuse of data registers.

sources.institution: Journal of Information, Law & Technology (JILT), University of Warwick — Andrés Guadamuz
sources.title: Habeas Data: The Latin-American Response to Data Protection (JILT 2000(2))
sources.quote: Habeas Data is a constitutional right granted in several countries in Latin-America.

sources.quote: This is a subcategory of the procedure enshrined in the Constitution for the protection of constitutional rights and therefore makes the protection of personal data a fundamental right.
sources.note: The web.archive.org URL failed repeatedly (connection reset) and EUR-Lex returns a bot challenge (HTTP 202). L 168/20, i.e. recital (7), so the title's 'recital 7' is correct. Date 30 June 2003 confirmed.

sources.quote: Following the Brazilian example, Paraguay incorporated the Habeas Data right to its new Constitution in 1992. After that, many countries followed suit and adopted the new legal tool in their respective constitutions: Peru in 1993, Argentina in 1994, Ecuador in 1996, and Colombia in 1997.

policyModels.name: Regional harmonisation (the African route)
policyModels.description: Regional communities write model or binding texts, and member states adopt or update national laws and authorities to match: ECOWAS's binding Supplementary Act (2010), the SADC Model Law (2012), and the continental Malabo Convention (2014, in force 2023). The texts borrow heavily from the European model, adapted to regional institutions. Some states legislated before the regional texts: Cabo Verde (2001) came first, followed by Burkina Faso and Mauritius (2004), Senegal (2008) and Benin (2009).
exemplars: ECOWAS states (e.g. Senegal, Ghana, Benin, Côte d'Ivoire, Nigeria)
SADC states (e.g. South Africa, Zambia, Zimbabwe, Botswana)
Malabo Convention parties (e.g. Rwanda, Mauritius, Senegal, Ghana)

myths.claim: Privacy is a Western idea, exported to the rest of the world with European law.
myths.correction: The first data-protection statutes were European, but concern for privacy is much older and wider. In the 2017 Puttaswamy judgment, India's Supreme Court rejected the argument that privacy is an 'elitist construct', and Justice Bobde's concurring opinion traced a well-developed sense of privacy in ancient Indian texts and in Islam. A Tokyo court recognised a right to privacy in 1964, drawing on American theory rather than European law, and Latin America built its own constitutional remedy, habeas data, from 1988. European laws were already a minority of the world's data-privacy laws by 2017, and by March 2025 Greenleaf counted 172 countries with such laws.

issues: Misattribution. The correction says 'India's Supreme Court, rejecting the argument that privacy is an elitist construct, traced a well-developed sense of privacy in ancient Indian and Islamic sources'. The 'elitist construct' rejection is in Chandrachud J's plurality (Part O, 'Not an elitist construct'). The ancient-texts and Islam passages (para 23) are in S.A. The Tokyo 1964 example cuts against the correction as written. The record's own JILPT source says Japan adopted the American 'right to be let alone' concept 'after the introduction of this theory by academics in the 1960s'. So the ruling shows an imported (American) idea, not an indigenous one. It still rebuts 'exported with European law', so it is kept and reworded to say so.

'172 countries ... most of them outside Europe' and 'habeas data from 1988' had no source on this record. Sources are added: Greenleaf/PL&B 2025 (172 by March 2025), Greenleaf/PL&B 2017 ('European laws (54/120) are a decreasing minority') and Guadamuz (Brazil 1988).

myths.correction: The German state of Hesse passed the first data-protection law in 1970 and Sweden the first national one in 1973. The GDPR replaced a 1995 EU Directive and has shaped many laws since, but it came nearly half a century after the first.

myths.claim: Most countries have no privacy or data-protection law.
myths.correction: Greenleaf's census counted 172 countries with national data-privacy laws by March 2025, and new laws have been added at 5.4 a year since 2020. His count includes some jurisdictions that are not UN members (in 2018, 112 of his 124 were UN member states), so it is not a straight comparison with the 193 UN member states, but a majority of UN members already had such laws by 2018 (112 of 193) and the share has grown since. Coverage and enforcement vary widely, and some large states (for example Pakistan) still have only a bill, but having no law at all is now the exception.

myths.claim: Africa has hardly any data-protection law; it is a latecomer.
myths.correction: Cabo Verde legislated in 2001, and Tunisia, Burkina Faso, Mauritius, Senegal and Benin followed in the 2000s. West Africa's ECOWAS bound its members to harmonised laws in 2010, and the AU's Malabo Convention entered into force in 2023. Of the ten national laws that Greenleaf and Cottier newly counted between January 2019 and February 2020, six were African. By January 2024, 36 of Africa's 55 countries had a data-protection law. In most countries the gap is now enforcement: many regulators lack independence and the resources to act on violations.

The 2000s laws check out on Data Protection Africa's fact sheets: Tunisia Organic Act 2004-63, Burkina Faso Law 010-2004/AN, Mauritius Data Protection Act 2004, Senegal Law 2008-12 and Benin Law 2009-09. The ECOWAS Supplementary Act A/SA.1/01/10 was signed at Abuja on 16 February 2010, and its Article 2 obliges each Member State to set up a legal framework. For the enforcement gap, Data Protection Africa (updated February 2024) says many countries with laws face 'resource and capacity constraints to enforce violations'. The same page gives a scale figure that answers the myth directly: 36 of 55 African countries had a law as of January 2024.

Everything else checks out. Cabo Verde's Law 133/V/2001 (2001) was Africa's first comprehensive law, and the Malabo Convention entered into force on 8 June 2023. All three existing quotes are verbatim.

myths.claim: Authoritarian states such as China and Russia have no data-protection law.
myths.correction: Russia adopted its Federal Law 'On Personal Data' (No. 152-FZ) on 27 July 2006. China's Personal Information Protection Law was passed on 20 August 2021 and gives individuals the right to access, copy, correct and request erasure of their personal information. These laws bind companies strictly but sit alongside broad state access and data-localisation rules: Russia has required citizens' data to be stored on Russian databases since 2015, and China requires critical-infrastructure operators and large processors to store data domestically. Anu Bradford calls China's approach to digital regulation a distinct 'state-driven' model. It is a different kind of regulation, not an absence of law.

issues: The correction's opening clause is wrong. 'Work under the ITU–EU HIPSSA project began around 2010' is contradicted by the record's own ITU document: its foreword says HIPSSA ran 'from the very beginning of the project in December 2008'. The earliest SADC data-protection text found is the ITU 'DRAFT ... SADC MODEL LAW ON DATA PROTECTION', dated March 2011. No source shows any 2010 text or 2010 start of drafting.
The existing quote covers only the Mauritius adoption. The Gaborone validation (27 February to 3 March 2012) is in the sentence just before it, so the quote is widened to cover both.

The verdict should be FALSE, not MISLEADING. No part of 'dates from 2010' is supported: drafting is first attested in March 2011, validation was in March 2012, ministerial adoption in November 2012 and ITU publication in 2013. A 2010 date may come from confusion with the ECOWAS Supplementary Act of February 2010.

Independent check: the Future of Privacy Forum's 2024 report on African RECs cites 'The SADC Model Law (2012)'. The SADC model laws on e-transactions and cybercrime carry the same Gaborone 2012 validation and Mauritius November 2012 adoption text. The Windhoek 2011 validation found in search results belongs to a different SADC text (a universal-service toolkit), not the data-protection model law.

issues: The quote is verbatim (--check FOUND), but it does not support the label 'Countries whose privacy authorities drafted the Madrid Resolution'. The 'fifty countries' sentence comes from the promotional preface signed by Artemi Rallo Lombarte, Director of the Spanish Data Protection Agency, and no list of the fifty is given.

The same PDF records who actually drafted the text. The AEPD invited every accredited authority to join a preparatory Working Group. The group met in January and June 2009 and drafted the Joint Proposal. Its footnoted membership list, 'AUTHORITIES BELONGING TO THE WORKING GROUP', names 23 authorities from 17 countries or territories, plus the European Data Protection Supervisor. The 17 are Austria, Belgium, Burkina Faso, Canada (2), Czech Republic, France, Germany (3), Hong Kong, Ireland, Italy, Netherlands, New Zealand, Portugal, Slovenia, Spain (4), Switzerland and the UK. So the formal drafters came from 17 jurisdictions, not 50. The 50 is the Spanish DPA's own broader count of the countries whose 'privacy guarantors' contributed.
The source institution should name the author of the quoted preface: the AEPD Director, writing for the Conference.

issues: All points and quotes check out. All five quotes, including the inline point sources, are verbatim on the free PL&B abstract pages (--check FOUND): 76 (1st ed. 2011), 109 (Jan 2015), 120 (Jan 2017), 132 (Jan 2019), 145 (Jan 2021), 157 (mid-March 2022), 162 (Feb 2023) and 172 (March 2025). The note's example of a recount is wrong. It says 'the 2020 decade recount gives 142 by end-2019 vs 132 in the January 2019 edition' to show that recounts are higher 'for the same years'. The two figures describe different cut-offs, January 2019 and end-2019. The PL&B February 2020 abstract says the 10-law gap consists of laws 'enacted or located' since January 2019, so much of it is new 2019 enactments, not recounting. A true same-period example comes from the same abstract: its per-decade counts (10 + 10 + 20 + 40) give 80 countries by end-2009, more than the 76 the 1st edition found in 2011.
The claim that counts include some self-governing territories is supported. The February 2020 abstract refers to 'over 200 countries (including self-governing territories)'. Source added.
